prs.title: Require Python 3.11 for Gradio 7, remove compatibility code, and allow Pillow 13
prs.body:
## Description

Require Python 3.11+ for Gradio 7 and the accompanying Python client. Python 3.10 reached end of life on [October 1, 2026](https://peps.python.org/pep-0619/). This PR targets **7.0-dev**, as requested.

- Update package metadata/classifiers, custom-component scaffolding and its preview fixture, CI jobs, development container, Docker tests, installation guides and contributor instructions.
- Import `NotRequired`, `ParamSpec` and test `Self` from `typing`; remove the client's direct `typing_extensions` dependency. Keep Gradio's dependency because Pydantic still needs the `TypedDict` backport on Python 3.11.
- Simplify timeout handling now that `asyncio.TimeoutError` aliases `TimeoutError`, and use `datetime.UTC`.
- Regenerate test requirements for Python 3.11, removing `exceptiongroup` and `backports-asyncio-runner` without unrelated package upgrades. Pillow is separately updated as described below. Make the Unix generation script explicitly resolve for 3.11. Keep `tomli` where coverage still requires it and `tomlkit` for TOML writing.
- Allow Pillow 13 with `pillow>=8.0,<14.0`, unblocking the patched release requested in #13999. Pin tests to Pillow 13.0.0 and exempt Pillow from the seven-day dependency delay so CI can exercise the recent release. This widens the upper bound; it does not require all users to upgrade to Pillow 13.
- Reject I-mode (32-bit integer) PIL images when encoding PNG on all supported Pillow versions, with an actionable error instead of silently clipping values. Explain explicit 16-bit conversion and lossless TIFF downloads in the new Gradio 7 migration guide.
- Leave the overlapping asyncio loop initialization cleanup to #13969.

Closes: #14004
Closes: #13999

## AI Disclosure

- [x] I used AI (Codex) to audit compatibility code, implement and self-review the changes, run validation, and write this description. Human review remains required before merging.
- [ ] I did not use AI

## 🎯 PRs Should Target Issues

Linked issue #14004 was created after checking open issues and PRs for overlapping minimum-version work.

## Testing and Formatting Your Code

Validated in a fresh Python 3.11 environment:

- Both package wheels build; their metadata requires Python >=3.11, excludes 3.10, and the client no longer declares typing_extensions.
- Client utility and datetime tests: **154 passed**.
- Pillow 13.0.0 on Python 3.11: **90 passed** across image utilities, Image, ImageEditor, Gallery and processing utilities. Wheel rebuild and metadata check confirm Pillow 13 is permitted and Pillow 14 is excluded. Formatting scripts rerun: Ruff passes; backend type checking reports 36 diagnostics and frontend type checking still reports 16 errors/400 warnings.
- API schema, chatbot, image editor, textbox and custom-component CLI tests: **121 passed, 1 xfailed**, plus one pip-discovery failure because uv created the environment without pip. Installed pip and reran that test successfully.
- API schema/history/datetime/client-state/route run: **343 passed**, stopped at 3 URL-handling failures. All three failures reproduce on the unchanged parent commit in the same Python 3.11 environment (baseline URL-test selection: 17 passed, 4 failed). Server tests used existing local frontend assets.
- Ran `bash scripts/run_backend_tests.sh`: collection blocked by missing vega_datasets, email-validator and transformers in the local environment. The first two were subsequently installed for focused tests; the full suite is not claimed green.
- Ran `bash scripts/format_backend.sh`: Ruff fixed the Python 3.11 modernization changes; subsequent lint and format checks pass. Type checking reported 42 diagnostics, mostly missing optional ML packages, plus unresolved BlocksMeta/BLOCKS_EVENTS imports.
- Ran `bash scripts/format_frontend.sh`: frontend type checking reported 16 errors and 400 warnings; no frontend application source is changed.
- Manually verified the new I-mode PNG error (including uppercase PNG), explicit 16-bit PNG round trips, lossless signed 32-bit TIFF round trips, and unaffected RGB/RGBA PNG encoding. No new automated tests were added, as requested. Formatting scripts rerun with the same 36 backend diagnostics and 16 frontend errors; targeted Ruff checks pass.
- `git diff --check` passes.

Draft pending human review and CI.

prs.title: Remove `gradio sketch` and the vibe editor
prs.body:
## Description

Targets `7.0-dev`. Removes `gradio sketch` and the vibe editor (`gradio --vibe`) ahead of Gradio 7.

**`gradio sketch`**
- In Gradio 6 the command was already a stub that only raised a `DeprecationWarning`. This PR deletes `gradio/cli/commands/sketch.py` and removes the command from the CLI. Its frontend code was already gone.
- Running `gradio sketch` now raises a short error saying it was removed, so people following old tutorials aren't sent into reload mode.
- The Gradio 6 migration guide's note about `gradio sketch` is left as is.

**Vibe editor**
- Backend: removes the `/vibe-edit`, `/undo-vibe-edit`, `/vibe-code` and `/vibe-starter-queries` routes with their request models and prompt helpers, the `vibe_mode` config value, the vibe analytics event, and the Hugging Face login (`hf_login.py`) and Ctrl+C auto-logout, which only vibe mode used.
- Frontend: removes the `@gradio/vibeeditor` package, its lazy loading and side panel in `Blocks.svelte`, and `vibe_mode` from the JS client's `Config` type.
- `gradio --vibe` now raises an error saying it has been removed.
- Setting `GRADIO_VIBE_MODE` now shows a `UserWarning` saying it no longer does anything. It shows once per process, even though the app is created several times per launch and again on every reload.
- Docs: the README and quickstart no longer mention vibe mode, and its sections are removed from the reload-mode guide and the environment variables guide (later entries renumbered).

Closes: #13913
Closes: #12674

prs.title: [Exploration] Gradio 7 default theme and component redesign
prs.body:
Exploration of a new Gradio 7 look. References: Vercel (monochrome, crisp, Geist), Apple (soft depth, generous radii) and ComfyUI (near-black canvas with tonal panels in dark mode).

## What changes

**Theme (`gr.themes.Default`)**
- Geist / Geist Mono, bundled locally (OFL) to match the offline-fonts work
- Grey canvas with borderless white cards and layered soft shadows; dark mode is `#0a0a0a` canvas, `#171717` panels and hairline borders
- Filled inputs that gain a border on hover and an orange focus ring
- Black pill primary button with an inner highlight and press scale; white ring-shadow secondary; Stop is red text instead of a red slab
- Orange is now reserved for focus states

**Components** (structure only; colors come from theme variables, so every theme inherits the new shapes)
- Slider: 8px track, floating 22px thumb that grows while dragging, value in a pill
- Radio: segmented control
- CheckboxGroup: pill chips
- Tabs: segmented pill instead of an underline
- Chatbot (bubble layout): user message in a filled bubble, assistant reply as plain text; message actions fade in on hover
- Toolbars: frosted floating pill
- Block labels: plain captions, no chip or icon
- Label: full-width track with the confidence filled in
- Accordion: chevron instead of ▼
- Upload: icon in a soft circle
- Dataframe header: quieter
- `h1`/`h2`: larger, tighter tracking

**New theme variables:** `slider_track_color`, `chatbot_user_background_fill`, `chatbot_user_text_color`, `checkbox_check_dark`

**Compatibility:** the previous default is kept as `gr.themes.Classic()`.

## Not done yet
- Dropdown menu, gallery, audio, video, number and the rest of the dataframe
- Hardcoded colors in the standalone dataframe and API docs
- Checking the other built-in themes (Soft, Ocean, etc.) against the new component shapes; Classic has been checked

prs.title: Record each user's run from a batched event to their own run history bucket
prs.body:
## Description

With `batch=True`, the queue runs requests from several users as one call. When run history is saved to an HF bucket, that call was recorded once, with every user's inputs and outputs, in the bucket of the first request in the batch. The other users' buckets got nothing. The queue built the batched call from the first event only: `compile_gr_request` returned a one-element list holding that event's request, and `call_process_api` passed the whole zipped batch to the recorder, which resolves the bucket and token from `request[0]`.

The queue now passes one `gr.Request` per event for a batch, in the same order as the batched data, and the recorder splits a batched call into one run per sample, each recorded with the request that sent it. The split only applies to functions declared with `batch=True`, so a client sending `"batched": true` to any other function is recorded as before.

Two smaller changes come with this. A batch with a single event was saved in column shape (`inputs=[["x"]]`), so loading it put a list into the component; it is now saved like any other run. A direct `/run/<api_name>` POST with `batched: true` has one caller for every sample, so each sample is now recorded to that caller's bucket as its own run instead of one combined record. If the requests and samples do not line up in any other way, nothing is recorded and a warning is logged, so a sample is never saved under someone else's request.

Browser storage was not affected, since each browser saves only its own run.

Not covered:

- A batch function still receives the first event's `gr.Request` and `gr.OAuthToken`, as before. That is separate from run history and left for a separate issue.
- A `.stream()` listener with `batch=True` loses its batched flag after the first chunk, because each chunk replaces the event's body. Those later calls are now skipped by the recorder instead of being filed under the first user. The batched streaming path has other problems unrelated to run history, so it is left for a separate issue.
- Each sample is its own recorder task now. The write pool's saturation check still keeps or drops a whole batch together, as before, but a batch's assets are now prepared per sample in parallel. That check never limited the asset step to begin with, so tightening it belongs in `history.py`.
- A `/run` POST with `batched: true` makes one bucket write per sample (at most `max_batch_size`), the same as sending the samples one by one. Grouping one caller's samples into a single write would need a multi-record save in `history.py`.

This touches the `_record_run_history` call in `route_utils.py` that #13979 and #13981 also change, so whichever merges last will need a small conflict fix.

Closes: #13984

prs.title: Don't rerun a `.stream()` handler on its last chunk when the stream ends
prs.body:
## Description

A `.stream()` event (microphone `gr.Audio` or webcam `gr.Image`) runs its handler once per chunk. When the user pressed Stop while the queue was waiting for the next chunk, the handler ran one more time on the chunk it had already processed, so side effects such as appending to `gr.State`, writing to a database or running a model happened twice for the last chunk.

`/stream/{event_id}/close` wakes the waiting stream through `event.signal` so it ends without waiting for the timeout. The stream loop in `process_events` treated every wake-up as a new chunk: it read `event.data` again, which still held the last chunk, called the handler, and only then checked `is_finished`. A close that arrives while the handler is running was already fine, since `is_finished` is checked right after that call and the stream ends there. The loop now checks the events right after the wait, and when every one of them is finished, it ends with the previous response instead of calling the handler again. The event stays in `awake_events`, so it completes as before (`process_completed` with the last output, and a successful run in the analytics) rather than going through the timeout path, which counts it as cancelled.

Closing the tab had the same problem. The heartbeat disconnect handler set `run_time` to infinity and woke the stream, which with `time_limit=None` (the default) is not `is_finished`, so the handler ran again on the last chunk and the event then held its slot until the 30 second wait timed out. It now also sets `event.closed`, like `/close` does, so the stream ends right away.

Closes: #13982

prs.title: Don't save runs started by a Timer tick or a page load to run history
prs.body:
## Description

Run history saves every call to a public endpoint, so a `gr.Timer` adds a run on every tick, and each page open adds one for `demo.load`, for every component with `value=fn`, and for `gr.LoginButton`'s login check. The browser keeps 100 runs per app, so these quickly push out the runs the user actually made, and in bucket mode each one is a Hub write.

This skips a run when its trigger is a `tick` or `load` event, including `.then()`/`.success()` steps chained after one. The check is per call, not per function: `gr.on([button.click, timer.tick], fn)` is still saved when the button is clicked. With `batch=True`, each event in a queued batch is checked against its own trigger, so a click and a tick that land in the same batch are handled separately. Calls without a `trigger_id` (`gradio_client`, custom frontends) are saved as before. The same rule runs in the browser (`client/js/src/utils/run_history.ts`) and in the server-side recorder (`gradio/route_utils.py`), next to the existing `api_visibility` check, which is left alone so these endpoints stay on the API page.

`dependency.ts` sent `event_meta.target_id || null`, which turned the root Blocks id `0` into `null`, so load events reached the client and server without a `trigger_id`. It now uses `??`. `prepare_event_data` still gives `EventData.target = None` for load events, since it has its own `if target` check. The `.failure()` steps dispatched from the catch block also passed no `target_id`, so they fell back to a function id. They now get the trigger of the step that failed, like `.then()` and `.success()` already do. `cancel()` dispatched the steps chained after a cancelled run with the cancelled function's id as `trigger_id`, which run history would read as a block id: in `gr.on([btn.click, demo.load], slow).then(after)` with `slow` as fn 0, cancelling a click run made `after` look like a load run, so it was not saved. Each submission now remembers its trigger and `cancel()` passes it on. Since every dispatch now passes a `target_id`, the `original_trigger_id` fallback and `walk_after_to_original` were unreachable, so they are removed.

Not covered: a `.change` listener fired because an automatic run updated its component (for example `timer.tick(fetch, None, df)` with `df.change(plot, df, out)`) is still saved, since the change event cannot tell a backend update from a user edit. The same applies to `gr.BrowserState`, which fires `change` when it restores a stored value on page open. An existing quirk in `dependency.ts` can still misclassify a run: an `always_last` event deferred behind a running one is replayed with the running one's trigger (and `event_data`). For example, in `gr.on([slider.change, demo.load], fn)`, a slider change made while the load run is in flight is not saved. That is left for a separate fix.

This touches the same lines in `submit.ts` and `route_utils.py` as #13979, so whichever merges second will need a small conflict fix.

Closes: #13980

prs.title: Save a `.stream()` input event to run history once, with its last output
prs.body:
## Description

A `.stream()` event (microphone or webcam streaming) runs its handler once per chunk. With an HF bucket, run history saved every one of those calls, plus one more on Stop, each with that chunk as the input. With browser storage it was one run per stream, but the input saved was the first chunk only. This makes both destinations save one run per stream, with the last output and the event's inputs except the streamed component, whose input is saved empty.

- Backend: `call_process_api` recorded every call whose `is_generating` was false, which is how it skips a generator's intermediate yields. A stream handler that is not a generator returns `is_generating=False` on every chunk, since the queue only sets it from the stream's state after the call returns. The extra record on Stop came from the handler running once more on the last chunk, which #13983 has since fixed. The queue now calls it with `record_history=False` for stream events and records the event itself once when it ends (Stop, the time limit, or no new chunk before the timeout), with the last response. A closed tab usually ends through that timeout too; if the queue notices the disconnect while a chunk is still being processed, the stream is dropped and not recorded, as a normal generator would be. A direct call to a stream endpoint that does not go through the queue is still recorded once, with its inputs as sent, since there the input is the whole value and not a chunk. A stream that ends with an error, is cancelled, or is served entirely from `@gr.cache` is not recorded. `_record_run_history` is renamed to `record_run_history` since the queue now calls it.
- Browser: `submit()` saved the payload it was called with, which for a stream includes the first chunk. It now saves the streamed component's slot as `null`, both when the run starts and in the later `update_run_inputs`. `send_chunk` also updates the other inputs when they change mid-stream, so they match the last output, as the server's record does.

A chunk is not the run's input and the stream itself is never kept, so loading one of these runs puts back the other inputs (a threshold slider, for example) and the output, and leaves the streamed component empty. Generators on normal events are unchanged: they are still saved once with their final value.

Closes: #13978

prs.title: Don't flash the app view before showing a Workflow Space's owner the canvas
prs.body:
## Description

When the owner of a `gr.Workflow` Space opens it while signed in, the page shows the app view for a moment and then switches to the workflow canvas.

On a Space the frontend has no way to know synchronously whether the visitor can edit: sign-in lives in an HttpOnly session cookie, and only the server's `get_write_access` answer settles it. The view picker therefore guessed "app" on Spaces, and the owner watched the page switch.

This PR changes that:

- **On a Space, show Gradio's loading indicator until the server answers.** Then show the right view. For visitors who aren't signed in, the answer comes back right away (no HF call is made). If it hasn't arrived after 3s, the page falls back to the app view.
- **Keep the app column hidden by CSS until a view is chosen.** The rule ships in the stylesheet `gr.Workflow` launches with (`#workflow-app:not([data-view="app"])`), and the canvas component sets `data-view` once it picks a view. So the app can't paint before that point, whatever order the components mount in. The App/Workflow toggle is likewise hidden until then.
- **Local runs are unchanged.** They still pick their view immediately from the write token in the URL or cookie.

Verified locally with a test-only build that treats `*.localhost` as a Space, and with `get_write_access` slowed to 1s. I recorded the app/canvas state every frame from page load:
- Owner: app never painted; the loading indicator, then the canvas once the answer arrived (~1.1s).
- Visitor: app shown when the answer arrived; canvas never painted.
- Plain local run (not a Space): owner gets the canvas in ~0.1s and a visitor gets the app in ~0.15s, without waiting on the check.

prs.title: forward ZeroGPU X-IP-Token from gr.Workflow + stop reporting quota errors as GPU unavailable
prs.body:
## Description

zerogpu spaces in a workflow were failing with "GPU quota exceeded" / "GPU unavailable" even when the user had quota left, while the same space worked fine when used directly 

the cause: zerogpu decides whose quota to charge (and queue priority) from the `X-IP-Token` header. the js client only attaches it to queued submits, but the canvas ran space nodes through a component server call, so every call reached the space anonymously and charged the workflow space's shared quota instead. thought this was addressed in #13747 but alas 

this pr:
- forwards the visitor's `x-ip-token` from `call_space` to the space
- runs space nodes through a queued `/call_space` endpoint so the header is actually sent
- relays the space's own queue messages ("Waiting for a GPU to become available", "Successfully acquired a GPU") as toasts on the canvas, so a gpu wait doesn't look like a hang
- fixes `_classify_error` so real quota errors ("You have exceeded your free ZeroGPU quota… Try again in 2:13:00") show as quota exceeded rather than "GPU unavailable — try again in a minute". zerogpu titles a queue timeout "quota exceeded" too, so that message is matched first
- shows the space's full error message in the node banner under the headline, since it says whose quota ran out and when it resets

prs.title: Speed up frontend updates in apps with many components
prs.body:
## Description

In an app with many components, every event slowed down by an amount that grew with the number of components earlier events had updated. This was reported in [this comment on #13934](https://github.com/gradio-app/gradio/issues/13934#issuecomment-6110243142).

Closes: #13934

**Root cause.** On each status message (pending, progress, complete), `DependencyManager.update_loading_stati_state()` pushed a loading status to *every* component that had ever had one. `LoadingStatus.current` only grows. For each of those components, `AppTree.update_state()` found the node by walking the whole tree (`find_node_by_id`), then awaited `get_data` on the component and all its descendants. After one event that updates many components (like loading a preset), every later event, even a one-output button, paid that cost several times over.

**Fix.**
- `update_loading_stati_state()` pushes only the statuses that changed since they were last pushed. It pushes all of them after a reload, when components are remounted. To make "changed" detectable, `LoadingStatus.update()` no longer replaces another event's entries that have nothing to reset, so those entries keep their identity.
- `AppTree` looks up nodes and their parents in an id index instead of walking the tree. The index is rebuilt lazily after `postprocess()` or a `gr.render` re-render replaces part of the tree.

**Behavior that relied on the full re-push, kept the same:**
- **`gr.render`:** a re-render rebuilds the block's components without a loading status. Before, the full re-push that followed restored it. Now the rebuilt components' status is pushed again once they are mounted, so an event still running for them keeps its progress indicator.
- **Clearing validation errors at the start of an event:** this keeps the input's current status instead of replacing it, so an input that is also pending for another event keeps its spinner.

## Measurements

The benchmark demo below runs under Chromium on an M-series Mac. Rows are 4× CPU-throttled unless marked otherwise, with 24 events per row. "update_state ms/event" is CPU-profile time inside `AppTree.update_state`. Latency is click to visible output (median). "Preset loaded" means the **Load preset** button (updates every extra field) was clicked once before measuring.

| Page | Event | update_state ms/event (main → PR) | Latency ms (main → PR) |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0 extra components | pick model (51 outputs) | 25.1 → 10.5 | 210 → 186 |
| 0 extra components | save (1 output) | 21.2 → 3.0 | 91 → 72 |
| 240 extra in tabs | pick model | 24.1 → 10.9 | 244 → 243 |
| 240 extra in tabs | save | 19.6 → 2.8 | 92 → 81 |
| 240 extra in tabs, **preset loaded** | pick model | **273.4 → 10.5** | **421 → 223** |
| 240 extra in tabs, **preset loaded** | save | **268.1 → 2.6** | **207 → 91** |
| 240 extra rendered, **preset loaded** | pick model | **467.2 → 10.5** | **783 → 322** |
| 240 extra rendered, **preset loaded** | save | **459.8 → 2.6** | **423 → 118** |
| 480 extra in tabs, **preset loaded**, no throttling | pick model | **185.4 → 2.4** | **271 → 83** |
| 480 extra in tabs, **preset loaded**, no throttling | save | **186.4 → 0.5** | **121 → 33** |

On `main`, every event after the preset load costs a few hundred ms more. With this PR the cost is about the same as before the preset was loaded.

## Verification

- `npx vitest run --config .config/vitest.config.ts js/core js/statustracker`: 67 passed. Each new test fails without the part of the change it covers (push only changed statuses, re-push after `gr.render`, keep pending status when clearing validation errors).
- Playwright (chrome): `render_heavy_concurrently render_merge render_queue_false sub_block_render accordion_tab_switch dataframe_tab_select invisible_textbox show_progress_on tabs validator_chatinterface validator_test visibility_test chatbot_editable test_chatinterface_streaming_echo` gave 49 passed and 2 failed. The 2 failures are in `test_chatinterface_streaming_echo` and fail the same way on unmodified `main` locally.
- Browser checks run on `main` and on this PR, with identical results:
  - A slow event whose outputs are inside a `gr.render` block, re-rendered while it runs: the outputs keep the "processing" indicator through the re-render and get their values.
  - A slow event whose outputs mount mid-run (switching to their tab, opening their accordion): they show the indicator, then their values.

## Demo (not committed)

Run with `EXTRA=240 EXTRA_LAYOUT=tabs python demo_issue_13934.py`. Click **Load preset**, then switch models or click **Save**.

```python
"""A large settings-style app: picking a model shows/hides and refills many
controls, like a trainer UI. EXTRA controls the number of extra components on
the page that the events never touch."""

import os
import time

import gradio as gr

MODELS = [f"Model {i}" for i in range(12)]
GROUPS = 6  # each model shows one group of option controls
PER_GROUP = 8
EXTRA = int(os.environ.get("EXTRA", "240"))
# "tabs": extras sit in four tabs (only the first is mounted);
# "visible": extras are all rendered on the page
EXTRA_LAYOUT = os.environ.get("EXTRA_LAYOUT", "tabs")


def pick(model):
    i = MODELS.index(model)
    updates = [f"### {model}\nSelected model #{i}."]
    for g in range(GROUPS):
        visible = g == i % GROUPS
        for j in range(PER_GROUP):
            updates.append(
                gr.update(visible=visible, value=f"{model} option {g}.{j}")
                if visible
                else gr.update(visible=False)
            )
    updates.append(gr.update(value=i * 3))
    updates.append(gr.update(value=i % 2 == 0))
    return updates


def save(name, lr, flag):
    return f"Saved preset {name!r} (lr={lr}, flag={flag}) #{time.time_ns()}"


with gr.Blocks(title="Trainer") as demo:
    header = gr.Markdown("### Pick a model")
    model = gr.Radio(MODELS, label="Base model", elem_id="model")
    option_boxes = []
    with gr.Row():
        for g in range(GROUPS):
            with gr.Column():
                for j in range(PER_GROUP):
                    option_boxes.append(
                        gr.Textbox(label=f"Option {g}.{j}", visible=g == 0)
                    )
    with gr.Row():
        lr = gr.Slider(0, 50, label="Learning rate")
        flag = gr.Checkbox(label="Use FP8")
    with gr.Row():
        preset = gr.Textbox(label="Preset name")
        save_btn = gr.Button("Save", elem_id="save")
        load_btn = gr.Button("Load preset", elem_id="load")
    status = gr.Markdown(elem_id="status")

    extras = []

    def extra_fields(t, n):
        for k in range(n):
            kind = k % 4
            if kind == 0:
                c = gr.Textbox(label=f"Field {t}.{k}")
            elif kind == 1:
                c = gr.Slider(0, 10, label=f"Value {t}.{k}")
            elif kind == 2:
                c = gr.Checkbox(label=f"Toggle {t}.{k}")
            else:
                c = gr.Dropdown(["a", "b", "c"], label=f"Choice {t}.{k}")
            extras.append(c)

    if EXTRA_LAYOUT == "tabs":
        with gr.Tabs():
            for t in range(4):
                with gr.Tab(f"Section {t}"):
                    extra_fields(t, EXTRA // 4)
    else:
        for t in range(4):
            with gr.Accordion(f"Section {t}"):
                with gr.Row():
                    for c in range(4):
                        with gr.Column():
                            extra_fields(f"{t}{c}", EXTRA // 16)

    model.change(pick, model, [header, *option_boxes, lr, flag])
    save_btn.click(save, [preset, lr, flag], status)

    def load_preset():
        values = []
        for c in extras:
            if isinstance(c, gr.Slider):
                values.append(5)
            elif isinstance(c, gr.Checkbox):
                values.append(True)
            elif isinstance(c, gr.Dropdown):
                values.append("b")
            else:
                values.append("from preset")
        return ["Preset loaded", *values]

    load_btn.click(load_preset, None, [status, *extras])

if __name__ == "__main__":
    demo.launch(server_port=int(os.environ.get("PORT", "7860")))
```

prs.title: Complete every job /cancel cancels, and let Job.cancel() cancel only its own job
prs.body:
## Description

`/cancel` cancels by `{session_hash}_{fn_index}`, so it kills every running job of that function in the session. Only the `event_id` in the request then got a `process_completed` message. The other cancelled jobs never completed: their ids stayed in the session's pending set and their clients waited until they timed out. Because the Python client puts all its jobs on one session hash, `job_one.cancel()` also killed `job_two`, which then hung.

The broad match itself is load-bearing. The frontend tracks only the latest submission of each function (`dependency.ts`'s `submissions` map), so with `trigger_mode="multiple"` a `cancels=` button relies on it to stop every in-flight run. So this PR makes two small changes and leaves that default alone:

1. **`/cancel` completes every job it cancels.** `cancel_tasks` already returns the event ids it cancelled. Each one now gets a `process_completed` message and has its iterator closed, the same as the requested event. This fixes the hang for every caller.
2. **The Python client cancels only its own job.** `CancelBody` gets an optional `only_event: bool = False`. When it's set, `/cancel` matches the full `{session_hash}_{fn_index}<gradio-sep>{event_id}` task name. `Job.cancel()` sends `only_event: True`. Older servers ignore the extra field, and older clients get the existing behaviour.

Tests:
- `client/python/test/test_client.py`: cancelling one of two concurrent jobs leaves the other running to completion. This is the issue's repro.
- `test/test_queueing.py`: a broad cancel of two running jobs sends `process_completed` for both. This test uses a real server, not `TestClient`, because `TestClient` runs requests on its own event loop where `/cancel` can't see the queue's tasks.

Both fail on `main`.

Closes: #13952

prs.title: Request an uncompressed body when /file= streams a remote URL
prs.body:
## Description

`/gradio_api/file=<url>` streams a remote file with `upstream.aiter_raw()` and passes through only a fixed set of headers, and `Content-Encoding` wasn't one of them. Because no `Accept-Encoding` was sent upstream, httpx added its default `gzip, deflate, br`. Any host that compresses (most CDNs, for JSON, text and SVG) sent back a gzip body, which Gradio then served labelled as the plain media type, so the client got a corrupted file.

This PR changes three headers. Only the 1st one is needed to fix the issue but I thought this is a good opportunity to fix all of them

- **Send `Accept-Encoding: identity` upstream.** Most hosts then send the file uncompressed, so the bytes Gradio streams are the file itself.
- **Pass `Content-Encoding` through.** `identity` is only a request, and some hosts ignore it. The common case is objects stored pre-compressed, such as S3 objects uploaded with `Content-Encoding: gzip`, which are served compressed whatever the client asks for. Passing the header through labels those raw bytes correctly, so the client decodes them. It's safe alongside the other headers: the forwarded `Content-Length` and `Content-Range` already describe the raw bytes, and Gradio's `BrotliMiddleware` skips any response that already has a `Content-Encoding`, so nothing is compressed twice.
- **Forward `If-Range` alongside `Range`.** A browser resuming a download sends both. Without `If-Range`, if the file had changed in between, the host would still return the requested range, and the browser would splice bytes from two different versions of the file. With it, the host returns the whole file instead.

The test in `test/test_routes.py` stands in for the host with an `httpx.MockTransport` that always gzips. It checks that the client gets the original body, and that `Accept-Encoding: identity`, `Range` and `If-Range` reach the host. It fails on `main`.

Closes: #13955

Targeting `7.0-dev` as there's a small chance as passing these headers could be a breaking change for some user

prs.title: Write gr.Video format conversions and watermarks into the cache
prs.body:
## Description

When `gr.Video` had to run ffmpeg in `_format_video` (a `format=` that differs from the returned file, or a `watermark=`), it chose the output path badly:

- **Format conversion (#13954):** the output was written next to the source with the new extension, and ffmpeg runs with `-y`. Returning `clip.webm` from a `gr.Video(format="mp4")` silently overwrote an unrelated `clip.mp4` in the user's folder.
- **Watermark (#13953):** rebuilding the name with `Path(...).stem + "_watermarked" + suffix` dropped the directory. The file landed in the process's working directory under a relative path, was never cleaned up, and two sessions whose uploads had the same filename overwrote each other's output.

Both now encode into a fresh temporary staging directory, then use `processing_utils.save_file_to_cache()` to store the output under its content hash. Identical outputs reuse the same cached file. Staging is removed on success and on encoding or caching failures. Output filenames are unchanged (`clip.avi`, `clip_watermarked.mp4`).

Two new tests in `test/components/test_video.py` cover this. One checks that a sibling file of the target name is left alone. The other checks that a watermarked output lands in the cache and not the working directory. Both fail on `main`.

Closes: #13953

prs.title: Escape LaTeX when restoring it into rendered markdown
prs.body:
## Description

A formula containing `<` was not rendered by `gr.Markdown` or `gr.Chatbot`, and the rest of the paragraph disappeared with it. `Bounds: $$a<b$$ and $$c>d$$ hold.` showed only `Bounds: $$a`.

`MarkdownCode.svelte` replaces each LaTeX block with a placeholder before running marked, so marked does not mangle it (#8822), and then puts the block back into marked's HTML output as is. A `<` inside the block therefore reached the browser unescaped. Here `<b$$ and $$c>` was parsed as an unknown element, and the sanitizer removed it together with its content.

The block is now escaped when it is put back, using the `escape()` helper already in `utils.ts`, in the mode that leaves existing entities alone (the same escaping marked applies to text). KaTeX auto-render reads the DOM text, so it still sees `<` and the formula renders. Because entities are kept, formulas that work around the bug with `<` (as in #10112) keep rendering as before. Since the `<` is now escaped before `escapeTags` runs, `allow_tags` no longer treats tag-like text inside a formula as a tag. One side effect: when the delimiters match text that is not meant as math (for example `$` around prices, if `$` is configured as a delimiter), raw HTML inside that span is now shown as text, the same way markdown inside it already was.

Closes: #13943

prs.title: Store gr.State in the browser so it works across replicas and restarts
prs.body:
## Description

`gr.State` lives in a single server process's memory today. As a result, apps that use it (including `gr.ChatInterface`, which passes chat history through `gr.State`) break when a request reaches a different replica, and lose state on every restart. This PR keeps `gr.State` values in the user's browser by default, with the server's memory used only as a cache.

**How it works**

1. After an event changes a `gr.State`, the server serializes the value and seals it into an encrypted, authenticated token (AES-GCM). It sends the token to the client together with a short reference: a keyed HMAC of the value.
2. The client sends that state with every event that reads or writes the `gr.State`. A token of 16KB or less is sent in full. A larger one is sent as its reference only.
3. If the server answering the event hasn't cached a referenced value (another replica served the last event, the process restarted, or the entry was evicted), it answers `409 {"missing_state": [ids]}` before queuing. The client then retries once, with the full tokens for those ids. The server never asks the client for state in the middle of an event.
4. The server's copy is a byte-bounded LRU cache (`GRADIO_STATE_CACHE_SIZE_MB`, default 256), so evicting an entry is always safe.

**Security**

- Tokens are sealed with a key derived from `GRADIO_SECRET_KEY`. Every replica needs the same value, and so does a process that should read tokens issued before a restart. Without it, each process uses a random key, which still works for a single process.
- Tokens and references are bound to the component id and to a fingerprint of the app's structure. A token for one State can't be replayed into another, or into a redeployed app where the same id means something else.
- References are keyed, so they can't be used to confirm a guess about a hidden value.
- A token that fails to verify resets that State to its initial value, with a one-time warning that points to `GRADIO_SECRET_KEY`.
- Known limit, documented in the guide: a user can send back an older token from their own session. Values that must not roll back, like credit balances, belong in a database.

**Serialization** (`gradio/state_serialization.py`)

- Uses tagged JSON, not pickle. Supported: JSON types, tuples, sets, dicts with non-string keys, bytes, dates, `Decimal`, `UUID`, paths, NumPy arrays and scalars, pandas DataFrames and Series (dtypes and indexes preserved), PIL images, dataclasses, pydantic models, enums, named tuples, and plain classes defined in the app's own code.
- Plain classes are rebuilt only if they are defined in the app's own code, not in the stdlib or an installed package. So even a leaked key can't instantiate arbitrary library classes.
- Values are compressed with zlib above 1KB.

**API changes for Gradio 7**

- `gr.State(storage="browser" | "server")`. The default is `"browser"`.
- If a value can't be serialized (e.g. it holds a lock or a model), it is kept in server memory with a one-time warning. If it becomes serializable again, it moves back to the browser.
- `time_to_live` is now enforced from the token's age. When it expires, the State resets to its initial value.
- `delete_callback` now requires `storage="server"`, since the server can't tell when a value kept in a browser is no longer needed. The internal example-preload States in `helpers.py`, and the two demos that use `delete_callback`, now set `storage="server"`.
- Changing a value in place (e.g. `history.append(x)` on an input-only State) is still saved: the server re-serializes the values an event touched and compares references.
- When concurrent events change the same State, the last one to finish wins.

**Compatibility**

Clients that don't send a `state` field keep the old server-side behavior. That covers older JS clients, the Python client, `/call`, and MCP. Batched events also keep the old behavior, since one batch mixes sessions.

**JS client** (`client/js/src/utils/state_store.ts`)

- Adds a token store. In browsers it is also saved to IndexedDB, keyed by app root and session hash, and pruned after 24h.
- On its own, this PR doesn't make state survive a page refresh, because a refresh still starts a new session. Once the Resume sessions PR, gradio-app/gradio#13585, reuses the session hash, `gr.State` comes back automatically.
- The client sends the state with each event, retries once on 409, and applies `output.state` before firing the data event, so the chained `.then()` events send the new state.

**Docs:** updated the state guides, the resource-cleanup guide, and the environment-variables guide (`GRADIO_SECRET_KEY`, `GRADIO_STATE_CACHE_SIZE_MB`).

**New dependency:** `cryptography`, for AES-GCM.

**Not in this PR**

- The Python client still uses server-side storage. It could adopt the same protocol later.
- Other per-process session state is unchanged: components changed with `gr.update`, `@gr.render`, and transport, which gradio-app/gradio#13925 handles.

Part of gradio-app/gradio#10487 and gradio-app/gradio#9136. Those issues also need gradio-app/gradio#13925 (transport) and stable `@gr.render` ids.

### Testing

- `test/test_client_state.py` (66 tests):
  - serializer round-trips, unsupported types, and refusal to rebuild library classes
  - sealing, tampering, scopes and keys
  - cache eviction
  - end-to-end runs through `/queue/join`: the cache-miss 409 and retry, simulated restarts, inline tokens, tampered and foreign tokens, the shared key, `time_to_live`, in-place mutation, stable callable defaults, the fallback for values that can't be serialized, `storage="server"`, legacy clients, generators, `.change` events, validators, and tokens copied to another component
- JS client: added `state_store.test.ts`. The node suite passes (184), and the browser suite passes (199).
- Full backend suite: 1361 passed. The failures that remain are environmental: `pip` isn't on PATH in a uv venv, and the docker tests need Docker.
- 61 Playwright specs that use State or chat interfaces all pass (`state_change`, `test_chatinterface_*`, `chatbot_*`, `render_*`, `unload_event_test`, `validator_*`, `kitchen_sink`, `todo_list`, …).
- Manually, in the browser: a counter, a growing 40KB random State, and a ChatInterface whose replies use the history. The small State was sent inline and the large one by reference.
- Manually, with a Node script on the built `@gradio/client`: it stayed connected while the server process restarted with the same `GRADIO_SECRET_KEY`. The counter continued from 4 to 5 and 6. The requests went 409 (reference to an uncached value), then 200 (retry with the token), then 200 by reference again.

## AI Disclosure

- [x] I used AI to write the implementation, tests, docs and this description (Claude Code), from a design discussed beforehand. It needs a careful human review before it is marked ready.
- [ ] I did not use AI

## Compatibility with gradio-app/gradio#13585 (Resume sessions)

This assessment is based on #13585 at `49e01bcb`.

**Summary.** The two PRs can be merged together and partly complement each other. The weak point is that they keep session data in different places. #13585 keeps it on the server: the browser holds only a session hash (in `sessionStorage`), and a refresh restores outputs from server memory via `/config?session_hash=`. This PR keeps `gr.State` in the browser so that it doesn't depend on one process. As things stand, the refresh feature from #13585 would still only work while the user stays on the same server process. To share one system, I think #13585 is the one to adjust, as described below. This PR needs only small fixes when merged.

### What already fits

- **Identifying the session.** This PR stores state tokens in IndexedDB under `root|session_hash`. The tab-scoped session hash from #13585 (with its `in_use`/duplicate-tab handling) is exactly the key that store needs. Once #13585 reuses the hash after a refresh, the restored client gets its `gr.State` tokens back with no further changes.
- **Resumed jobs.** A job that resumes after a refresh receives the same `process_generating`/`process_completed` messages, and those carry `output.state`. Applying state updates is idempotent, so messages replayed from the buffer are harmless.
- **Session lifetime.** The grace period before a session is deleted, and running `unload` only when the page doesn't come back, still matter for `storage="server"` values, running jobs and `unload`. A browser-held `gr.State` needs no cleanup on the server.

### Merge conflicts to resolve (textual, not design)

- **`client/js/src/utils/submit.ts`:** #13585 moves the message callback into `register_queue_event()`. The `state_store.apply(data.state)` call from this PR has to go there, before the `data` event, so that both new and resumed events apply it.
- **`client/js/src/client.ts`:** `state_store.attach(root|session_hash)` must run after `restore_session()`. That function can replace the session hash with a fresh one when this tab didn't own it.
- **`gr.State` docstring and guides:** both PRs edit the `gr.State` docstring (`time_to_live`), `state-in-blocks.md`, `interface-state.md`, and the environment-variables guide (both add an entry numbered 26). This PR keeps "refreshing resets state", because on its own a refresh still starts a new session. After both merge, that wording should become "refreshing keeps state".

### Where the designs differ, and what I'd change in #13585

1. **Restore outputs from the browser, not from server memory.**
   - `load_session()` reads the values from `app.state_holder[session_hash]`. After a restart, a replica switch, or the 1-hour state TTL, `session_restored` is `false` and the outputs are lost, even though the browser had them.
   - The frontend already holds every value it shows, so the client could save them next to the state tokens, in the same IndexedDB record keyed by `root|session_hash`, and restore them without a server round trip.
   - Two things remain tied to one server process:
     - File values: the URLs point at one server's cache, which needs the planned shared FileStore.
     - Components changed with `gr.update(...)`: their props live in the server's per-session copies, which also drive input validation.
   - Those per-session component copies are the next thing to move to the browser, as sealed blobs using the same `ClientState` mechanism from this PR. They don't have to block either PR.
2. **Don't tie the saved session to `app_id`.** `is_session()` requires `session.app_id === config.app_id`, but `Blocks.app_id` is `random.getrandbits(64)` for each process. So a refresh after a restart, or one that reaches another replica, discards the saved session hash, which also orphans the browser-held state saved under it. A stable identity would avoid this, such as the structure fingerprint this PR binds tokens to (`app_fingerprint`), or just `root`.
3. **Decide `session_restored` in the browser.** Load events are skipped when the server still had the session. With browser-held state, the question is whether the browser has saved values for this page. Otherwise, after a restart, the load events run again and overwrite the `gr.State` the browser just restored.
4. **Use one client-side storage module.** The two PRs would then share one browser-side storage system:
   - #13585's small per-tab pointer stays in `sessionStorage` (session hash, `in_use`, pages shown, resumable events).
   - The saved data goes in IndexedDB (state tokens, plus outputs once item 1 is done).
   - Both live in one module, rather than `utils/session.ts` and `utils/state_store.ts` side by side.
5. **Resuming a job still needs the same process.** Its buffered messages exist only on the replica running it. Neither PR changes this. For multiple replicas it needs sticky routing, or a follow-up on top of #13925 (one request per event). It's worth saying so in #13585's docs.

### What changes on this PR's side after both merge

- The two merge fixes above.
- Generalize `StateStore` into the shared session record from item 4.
- Update the guide text about refreshing.
- No protocol changes: the join payload, the 409 retry and `output.state` stay as they are.

prs.title: Render streamed markdown block by block instead of rebuilding the whole message
prs.body:
## Description

While a message streams into `gr.Chatbot` or `gr.Markdown`, every update re-rendered the entire message: `marked.parse` over the whole text, `sanitize()` parsed the result into a new `DOMParser` document and serialized it back to a string, and `{@html}` parsed that string again and replaced every node. The DOM work per update grows with the message length, so one streamed answer costs quadratic work and the browser builds up a large pile of garbage nodes during long answers. This follows the approach proposed in the issue, in two parts:

1. `sanitize_fragment()` in `@gradio/sanitize` parses the HTML once into a `<template>`, sanitizes it in place and returns the nodes, which `MarkdownCode` inserts directly. No document is created per update and the serialize/re-parse round trip is gone. `sanitize()` keeps its string API (used by toasts) and is built on top of it. Template contents belong to a document that lives as long as the page, so the amuchina patch from #13885 now walks fragments directly instead of creating a `NodeIterator` there, which would keep every sanitized fragment alive. Renders also run one at a time now, and updates that arrive during a render collapse into the latest message.
2. `MarkdownCode` lexes the text on every update but only renders, sanitizes and inserts the top-level blocks that changed. Blocks in the unchanged prefix and suffix keep their DOM nodes, and KaTeX only runs on the new blocks. Mermaid draws new diagrams on its own once the text has caught up, so text updates keep rendering while it loads or runs, and an invalid diagram does not stop later updates from rendering. A block is reused when its source and its heading ids are unchanged; when the reference link definitions or the render settings (`render_markdown`, `sanitize_html`, `allow_tags`, `latex_delimiters`, `theme_mode`) change, every block is rebuilt. Raw HTML can leave an element open across blocks (for example `<details>` wrapped around markdown), so blocks are grouped until that element is closed again and each group is parsed as one piece of HTML, as before. An inline tag in prose, such as `List<T>`, ends with its block as it does in the HTML parser, so it does not pull the rest of the message into one group. Tags that `allow_tags` escapes to text, such as a streamed `<think>` in a chatbot, are not counted as open elements either, so they do not pull the blocks after them into one group.

Streaming the markdown from the issue 3 words per update, counting nodes inserted under the message with a `MutationObserver`:

| Sections | Updates | Final nodes | Inserted (main) | Inserted (this PR) | `DOMParser` calls (main / this PR) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 10 | 161 | 630 | 49,460 | 2,590 | 161 / 0 |
| 20 | 321 | 1,260 | 199,720 | 5,180 | 321 / 0 |
| 40 | 641 | 2,520 | 802,640 | 10,360 | 641 / 0 |

For a fixture covering headings, lists, tables, highlighted code, LaTeX, reference links and raw HTML, a one-shot render produces the same HTML as `main` with and without `header_links` and `sanitize_html`, apart from heading ids (below). The same holds for raw HTML that spans blocks (`<details>` around markdown, nested `<div>`s, an unclosed `<b>`, an element that is never closed).

Behavior changes worth knowing about:

- Heading ids with `header_links=True` came from a module-level slugger that was never reset, so they changed on every re-render (`h-section`, then `h-section-1`, `h-section-2`, ...) and depended on whatever else had rendered on the page. They are now numbered per component in document order and stay stable. Two components that both contain `## Intro` now both get `h-intro`.
- Sanitizing now parses in template context instead of a `DOMParser` body. The only difference in the resulting DOM I found is that an HTML comment at the very start of a message is now kept instead of dropped. The only caller of the `sanitize()` string API is the toast, where this makes no practical difference.
- The browser sanitizer now drops `<meta>` elements, like `<style>` and `<link>`. Amuchina allows `<meta http-equiv>` by default, so a refresh pragma in a message could redirect the page. `DOMParser` used to move one at the very start of a message into a discarded `<head>`, which template parsing no longer does, but one later in the message already got through on `main`.
- KaTeX now runs per block, so a macro defined with `\gdef` in one block is not available in later blocks. On `main`, one pass over the whole message shared the macros.

The PR also fixes `optimizeDeps.include` in `js/spa/vite.config.ts`. Its entries belong to workspace packages and did not resolve from the repo root, so they were never prebundled. With a cold optimizer cache (here caused by the lockfile change from the amuchina patch) they were discovered mid-run, the forced reload hung vitest, and the `js-test` prewarm step timed out.

Closes: #13932

Its tag regex was narrower than what marked passes through as raw HTML, so some tags were never escaped and the sanitizer then removed them together with their content. Besides underscores (``), this also affected self-closing tags with no space (`before after` lost everything after the tag) and namespaced closing tags (``). prs.title: Preserve the alpha channel of images loaded into gr.ImageEditor (backport to 6.x)
prs.body:
## Description

This backports #13874 (merged into `7.0-dev` as 342c525) to `main`, so the ImageEditor RGBA fix ships in 6.x without waiting for 7.0. It's a straight `git cherry-pick -x`, which applied without conflicts. The only change is that I dropped the hand-written changeset so the bot generates one from this title. See #13874 for the full rationale.

Summary: `gr.ImageEditor` used to flatten loaded images onto an opaque background, so once you edited an RGBA image its transparent areas came back white. Now the background layer stays transparent when it holds an image, the editor shows a checkerboard behind transparent areas, and canvas export un-premultiplies alpha. `image_mode="RGB"` composites onto white, so RGB output doesn't change.

Behaviour changes carried over from #13874 (worth a look before shipping in a minor release):
- In the default RGBA mode, the padding around an image smaller than a `fixed_canvas` is now transparent instead of white.
- Handlers that drop alpha themselves (`x[..., :3]`, PIL `convert("RGB")`) now get the RGB values under transparent pixels instead of white.

Closes: #13935

**Verification** (on top of `main` @ 8c71eaaff)

Demo (not committed): a 200×200 RGBA image where the left half is opaque red and the right half is transparent. I drew a stroke on the red half, then read the alpha of the right half in the handler.

```python
import numpy as np
import gradio as gr

img = np.zeros((200, 200, 4), dtype=np.uint8)
img[:, :100] = [255, 0, 0, 255]

def inspect(value):
    bg, comp = value["background"], value["composite"]
    return f"background alpha (right half) max={bg[:, 120:, 3].max()} | composite alpha (right half) min={comp[:, 120:, 3].min()}"

with gr.Blocks() as demo:
    editor = gr.ImageEditor(value=img, type="numpy")
    btn = gr.Button("Inspect")
    out = gr.Textbox(label="Result")
    btn.click(inspect, editor, out)

demo.launch()
```

| | Canvas | Result after one stroke |
|---|---|---|
| `main` | right half shown white | `max=255 \| min=255` (transparency lost) |
| this PR | checkerboard on right half | `max=0 \| min=0` (transparency kept) |

- `pytest test/components/test_image_editor.py`: 4 passed
- `pnpm vitest run --config .config/vitest.config.ts js/imageeditor`: 65 passed, 1 failed. The failure is `brush-textures.test.ts › keeps repeated strokes of the same color at a fixed opacity`, which this PR doesn't touch. It fails the same way locally on unmodified `main`.

prs.title: Fix hidden Accordion revealed with open=True rendering empty
prs.body:
## Description

When an Accordion with `visible=False, open=False` is updated to `visible=True, open=True` in one event, its header renders open but its children never mount. The first header click then collapses what looks like an empty accordion.

**Root cause:** children of a closed accordion are not rendered at startup. They are rendered when the accordion fires `gradio_expand`, which it does from `set_data` when `open` changes. A hidden accordion is not mounted, so `update_state` stores `open=True` as a pending prop and the accordion later mounts already open. `set_data` never sees the change, so `gradio_expand` never fires.

**Fix:** in `update_state`, when an unmounted accordion is set to `open=True`, call `render_previously_invisible_children` for it directly.

Closes: #13881

prs.title: Let gr.Audio and gr.MultimodalTextbox pass media track constraints to the microphone
prs.body:
## Description

Microphone recording in `gr.Audio` always opened the mic with `getUserMedia({ audio: true })`, so there was no way to turn off the browser's echo cancellation, noise suppression or automatic gain control. As #5024 describes, those defaults can noticeably hurt recording quality with some headsets, and cameras already have a way to set this through `gr.WebcamOptions(constraints=...)`.

This PR adds a `gr.MicrophoneOptions` dataclass with a single `constraints` field, and a `microphone_options` parameter that takes it (or a dict) on `gr.Audio`, `gr.Microphone` and `gr.MultimodalTextbox`:

```python
gr.Audio(
    sources=["microphone"],
    microphone_options=gr.MicrophoneOptions(
        constraints={"echoCancellation": False, "noiseSuppression": False, "autoGainControl": True}
    ),
)
```

`constraints` is a `MediaTrackConstraints` dict for the audio track, not a full `MediaStreamConstraints` like `WebcamOptions.constraints` (`{"video": ..., "audio": ...}`), since there is only one track here. Nothing changes when it is not set: the mic is requested with exactly the same arguments as before, and no default constraints are changed.

On the frontend, the constraints are passed to every place that opens the microphone. In `gr.Audio` that is the `getUserMedia` call for streaming in `InteractiveAudio.svelte`, the waveform visualizer in `StreamAudio.svelte`, and both `startMic()` and `startRecording()` in `WaveformRecordControls.svelte`. `startRecording()` needs them too: the Record button calls it without opening the mic first, and `stopMic()` runs after every take, so it is usually `startRecording()` that opens the mic. wavesurfer's `RecordPlugin` (7.11.0) passes the object straight through as `getUserMedia({ audio })`, so no workaround is needed there. Constraints the device can't satisfy make the mic request fail with an `OverconstrainedError`, so `WaveformRecordControls` now catches a failed `startMic()` or `startRecording()` and reports it through `onerror` with `audio.recording_error`, as streaming `gr.Audio` already does. Before, the Record button silently did nothing in that case, and also when mic access was denied. In `gr.MultimodalTextbox`, `MinimalAudioRecorder` already passes the selected `deviceId`, so the constraints are merged with it. The device the component has selected (the first one found, or the one picked from its list) overrides a `deviceId` in the constraints. Since that first device is only known once mic permission has been granted, a `deviceId` constraint there is only honored before that; making it consistent would mean changing how the initial device is chosen, which I left out of this PR.

While working on this I noticed that the device dropdown in `gr.Audio` (`DeviceSelect.svelte`) does not actually select a device: its value is never read, and the mic is opened without a `deviceId`. That predates this PR and is left as is, but it means a `deviceId` constraint is currently the only way to choose the device in `gr.Audio`.

A `demo/microphone_constraints` demo is added, modeled on `demo/webcam_constraints`, and `MicrophoneOptions` is added to the Helper Classes on the Audio and MultimodalTextbox docs pages.

This targets `7.0-dev` since it adds new public API and the issue is on the Gradio 7 milestone.

Closes: #5024

prs.title: Make gr.Gallery's empty state respect `sources`
prs.body:
## Description

`gr.Gallery`'s empty state did not follow `sources`. With `sources=["webcam"]`, file upload still showed up even though it is not an allowed source (#13929), and the same root cause also made clear behave differently from deleting the last item, and left a clickable upload area on clipboard-only galleries. This PR makes the empty state follow two rules: it only offers allowed sources, and whenever the gallery is emptied it goes back to `sources[0]`, the same source it starts on.

1. **Toolbar upload button.** The upload button above a populated gallery was gated only on `upload && stream_handler`, which `Index.svelte` always passes. It now also requires `sources.includes("upload")`, like the webcam, video and clipboard buttons next to it. The button predates `sources` (#11787), and #12804 added the check only to the new buttons.

2. **Source after clear.** The clear button always called `onsource_change("upload")` (added in #12804, when upload was still the only empty state), so a webcam-only gallery fell back to the file upload area, and with `["webcam", "upload"]` clear landed on upload while deleting the last item landed on the webcam. Clear now resets `active_source` to `sources[0]`. Separately, the capture, upload and paste handlers leave `active_source` as `null`, so an `$effect` (following the one in `ImageUploader.svelte`) replaces an unset or disallowed source with `sources[0]`; that is what makes deleting the last item after a capture land on the right source.

3. **Clipboard-only empty area.** When `"upload"` is not allowed, clicking the empty area no longer opens the file picker, and in clipboard mode a click pastes from the clipboard (and the area is labelled as a paste target), as `ImageUploader` does. `BaseFileUpload` gets `disable_click` and `aria_label` props (passed through to `Upload`) for this. Drag and drop onto the area still works, also matching `ImageUploader`.

Behavior change: with a mixed order such as `sources=["webcam", "upload"]`, clear now returns to the webcam instead of the upload area. That matches what the component shows on first load and what deleting the last item already did. Nothing that user code sees changes (`value` and the `clear`/`change` events are the same).

Closes: #13929

prs.title: Fix Python client heartbeat connections that leak or reconnect in a tight loop
prs.body:
## Description

The Hugging Face Spaces proxy ran out of file descriptors (`Too many open files`) and returned 502s to every running Space until it was redeployed. Open sockets on the proxy were climbing steadily. The Python client's heartbeat was contributing in three ways, and this PR fixes all three. It supersedes #13927, which couldn't be updated because its branch is on a fork.

**1. Dropped clients never released their heartbeat.** The heartbeat thread held the `Client` strongly, so a client dropped without `close()` was never garbage collected. It kept a heartbeat connection open for the life of the process. The common case is a Space that creates `Client(...)` inside a request handler. The thread now holds the client weakly, and `__del__` stops it.

**2. Error responses were retried in a tight loop.** Any response that ended, such as a 404 from an app without the heartbeat route, a redirect or a 5xx, was reconnected immediately, at roughly 360 requests per second per client, each on a new connection. Every Python client talking to a Gradio app older than the heartbeat route (April 2024) did this for as long as it lived. The same loop also hammered the proxy while it was returning 502s and 429s. Now:
- a 4xx other than 429 (and a 3xx) stops the heartbeat, since retrying won't fix it;
- a 5xx, a 429, a 2xx that isn't `text/event-stream`, or a stream that ends is reconnected with exponential backoff from 1s to 60s. Brief streams that send an initial heartbeat and then end retain accumulated backoff; a connection must stay healthy for 30s before the delay resets.

**3. The heartbeat connected even when the app didn't need it.** The server's config sets `connect_heartbeat` only for apps with session state, `unload` events or streams. The JS client has honoured it since #8169, but the Python client connected for every app. The Python client now skips the heartbeat when the flag is explicitly false. Gradio 4.25–4.28 servers have a heartbeat route but lack the flag, so missing flags still connect to preserve state cleanup and unload callbacks. Servers without the route stop after one 404.

Measured locally against a stub heartbeat server (requests in 3s from one client):

| Heartbeat response | Before | After |
|---|---|---|
| 404 | 1085 | 1 (stops) |
| 307 redirect | 1092 | 1 (stops) |
| 200 HTML page | 1072 | 2 (backs off) |
| 502 ×3, then OK | 4 | 2 (backs off, then recovers) |

For 40 per-request clients dropped without `close()`: before, 40 heartbeat threads stayed alive forever. After, they all exit once garbage collected.

Closes: no public issue; this was reported internally from the Spaces proxy incident.

cc @christophe-rannou whose earlier PR was adapted for this.

prs.title: Mirror the webcam only for front-facing cameras by default
prs.body:
## Description

`gr.WebcamOptions(mirror=...)` was a fixed boolean that defaulted to `True`, so on phones the back camera was mirrored too, which makes text and scenes read backwards. This PR adds `mirror="auto"` and makes it the default for `gr.Image`, `gr.Video` and `gr.ImageEditor`. `gr.Gallery` has no `webcam_options` and always mirrored its webcam, so it now uses `"auto"` too. In auto mode the webcam is mirrored unless the browser reports the active track's `facingMode` as `"environment"`. The value is re-read when the user switches cameras. Desktop webcams report `"user"` or nothing, so they stay mirrored as before. `True` and `False` behave as they did.

I went with `facingMode` rather than the "back" substring in the device label suggested in the issue, since labels are localized and vendor-specific.

Recorded video needed one more piece. The browser records the raw stream and the backend flips it with ffmpeg afterwards, but the backend cannot know which camera was used. The frontend now sends the effective mirror state as `meta.mirrored` on the uploaded `FileData` (added as an optional key on `FileDataMeta`), and `Video.preprocess` flips based on it when webcam is one of the component's sources. Payloads without the flag (API and `gradio_client` callers) keep the old rule, with `"auto"` treated like `True`.

Two side effects of using the flag, both of which I think are fixes:

- With `sources=["upload", "webcam"]`, webcam recordings used to be shown mirrored but saved unmirrored, because the backend could not tell a recording from an upload and only flipped when webcam was the sole source. Recordings are now saved to match the preview. Uploaded files carry no flag and are still never flipped.
- The mirrored playback after recording now follows the recording's flag instead of `webcam_options.mirror`, so a video the app puts in the component while the webcam source is active is no longer shown flipped.

Not covered here: `gr.Gallery` saves webcam recordings unflipped, so a front-camera recording there still does not match its mirrored preview. Fixing that needs a flip in the Gallery backend, so I left it for a follow-up.

Since this changes a default, it targets `7.0-dev`.

Closes: #12876

Open these on a phone; desktop webcams never report a rear-facing camera.

prs.title: Fix 16-bit audio conversion of uint8, int8 and float16 arrays on NumPy 2
prs.body:
## Description

`convert_to_16_bit_audio` does its scaling in the input dtype. That worked on NumPy 1.x, where value-based casting silently upcast `uint8 * 257` to uint16, `int8 * 256` to int16 and `float16 * 32767` to float32. NumPy 2 (NEP 50) keeps the array dtype when the other operand is a Python scalar, so returning such an array from a function whose output is `gr.Audio` now fails:

- uint8 and int8 raise `OverflowError: Python integer 257 out of bounds for uint8` (256 for int8)
- float16 rounds 32767 up to 32768, so a full-scale positive sample wraps to -32768 when cast to int16

This PR widens the data explicitly before scaling (uint8 to int32, int8 to int16, float16 to float32). The output is identical to what NumPy 1.x produced, so the existing mappings and the silence handling from #13396 are unchanged (I also checked that the new test passes on NumPy 1.26.4, which CI does not run).

Closes: #13923

prs.title: Migrate the MCP integration to mcp v2
prs.body:
## Description

**Stacked on gradio-app/gradio#13920** (httpx → httpx2): this PR targets that branch, so the diff here is only the mcp v2 migration. Once #13920 merges into `7.0-dev`, retarget this PR to `7.0-dev`.

This moves Gradio's MCP integration from mcp 1.x to mcp 2.x. mcp 1.x is in maintenance mode (security fixes only), and mcp 2 uses `httpx2`, so after this change the `mcp` extra no longer pulls in `httpx`.

It also fixes a silent breakage in released Gradio. The `mcp` extra pins `mcp<2`, but plain `pip install gradio mcp` now installs mcp 2.2. With that install, `launch(mcp_server=True)` logs `Error launching MCP server: 'Server' object has no attribute 'call_tool'`. Gradio catches the error and keeps going, so the app looks fine, but `/gradio_api/mcp/` returns 404.

### Changes
- **`gradio/mcp.py`**, ported to the v2 low-level `Server`:
  - Handlers are passed as `on_*` constructor arguments, take `(ctx, params)`, and return full result types (`ListToolsResult`, `ReadResourceResult` with `TextResourceContents`/`BlobResourceContents`, …) instead of bare lists.
  - The helpers that used to read `self.mcp_server.request_context` (removed in v2) now take the request from `ctx`.
  - Model fields are snake_case (`input_schema`, `mime_type`, `structured_content`, `uri_template`, `meta`).
  - **Tool errors stay visible to the model.** In v2, an exception in `on_call_tool` becomes a JSON-RPC error, which clients raise instead of showing to the model. The handler catches exceptions and returns `CallToolResult(is_error=True)`, which is what v1's decorator did. To make that one `try/except`, the tool body moved into a `_call_tool` method, which is why the diff is larger than the logic change.
  - Progress uses `ctx.session.report_progress()`, which the migration guide recommends and which works on both protocol versions.
  - The SSE transport, the streamable-HTTP session manager, and all `/gradio_api/mcp` routes are unchanged.
- **`gradio upload-mcp`** and `demo/mcp_resources_and_prompts/fastmcp.py`: `FastMCP` → `MCPServer`. The CLI now raises `ToolError`, because v2's `MCPServer` hides other exceptions' messages (a file outside the allowed directory would otherwise report only "Error executing tool").
- **`requirements-mcp.txt`**: `mcp>=1.21.0,<2.0.0` + `pydantic>=2.11.10,<=2.12.5` → `mcp>=2.0.0,<3.0.0`. mcp 2 requires `pydantic>=2.12.0` itself. The `<=2.12.5` cap (from #12598) had no documented reason, and the tests pass on both 2.12.5 and 2.13.4.
- **Tests, benchmark, and guides**: moved to the v2 client API (`streamable_http_client`, `meta={"progress_token": ...}`, `tool.input_schema`) and `MCPServer`.

One behaviour change: v1's `call_tool` decorator validated arguments against the tool's input schema before calling it, and v2 removed that. Bad arguments now fail inside Gradio's own argument handling and come back as an `is_error` result, still visible to the model.

### Protocol compatibility
mcp 2 serves the new **2026-07-28** protocol and older **2025-era** clients from the same endpoint. The new test `test_mcp_tools_resources_and_prompts` is parametrized over both. Over both protocols it lists and calls tools (including a failing one, which returns `is_error`), lists and reads resources and resource templates (text and binary), and lists and fetches prompts. Checked by hand:

| | Protocol | Result |
|---|---|---|
| mcp 2 `Client` → streamable HTTP | 2026-07-28 | tools, progress (3 notifications), resources, prompts ✓ |
| `ClientSession` + `initialize()` → streamable HTTP | 2025-11-25 | ✓ (the path Cursor, Claude Desktop through `mcp-remote`, etc. use) |
| `sse_client` → `/gradio_api/mcp/sse` | 2025-11-25 | list and call tools ✓ |
| `gradio upload-mcp` over stdio | 2026-07-28 | upload ✓, file outside the directory → `is_error` with the reason ✓ |

### Verification
Python 3.10, installed in CI's order, with `mcp==2.2.0`:
```bash
python -m pytest test/test_mcp.py      # 17 passed (also on mcp 2.0.0 and 2.0.1, and on pydantic 2.12.5)
python -m pytest -n 8 -m "not flaky" test                        # 1304 passed
cd client/python && python -m pytest -n 8 -m "not flaky" test/   # 171 passed
ruff check gradio test client && ruff format --check gradio test client && ty check  # clean
python scripts/benchmark_latency_mcp.py   # same latency as mcp 1.x on #13920
```
As on #13920, the only local failures are environmental: 12 Docker reverse-proxy tests (no Docker daemon) and `test_get_executable_path` (`uv venv` has no `pip`).

prs.title: Migrate from httpx to httpx2
prs.body:
## Description

`httpx` is no longer maintained. [`httpx2`](https://github.com/pydantic/httpx2) is Pydantic's maintained fork with the same API. This PR moves `gradio` and `gradio_client` onto it for Gradio 7.

Gradio depends on `safehttpx`, which also used `httpx`. gradio-app/safehttpx#17 migrated it, and **`safehttpx` 0.2.0 is now on PyPI**. This PR requires it (`safehttpx>=0.2.0,<0.3.0`). Starting with 0.2.0, the `safehttpx` README says it uses `httpx2`, and that anyone who still needs `httpx` should pin `safehttpx<=0.1.7`.

Closes: #13705

### What's visible today
authlib 1.8 prefers `httpx2` and warns when it has to fall back to `httpx`. Released Gradio doesn't install `httpx2`, so every OAuth app (`gr.LoginButton`) on a Space logs the warning from the issue thread. This is a fresh `pip install "gradio[oauth]"` (6.28.0, which resolves `huggingface_hub` 1.33 and `httpx` 0.28.1, no `httpx2`), importing authlib the way `gradio/oauth.py` does on a Space:
```
authlib/integrations/httpx_client/assertion_client.py:5: AuthlibDeprecationWarning: The httpx module is deprecated; please use httpx2 instead.
```
With this branch and `safehttpx` 0.2.0 there is no warning. Nothing installs `httpx` unless `huggingface_hub<2`, `mcp<2` or another package still asks for it.

### Changes
- **Code:** every `import httpx` / `httpx.X` in `gradio/`, `client/python/`, the tests, `scripts/`, `demo/dia_dialogue_demo` and the Discord/Slack bot guides is now `httpx2`. The changes are purely mechanical: the public API is identical (I diffed the two packages' `__all__`: `httpx2` only adds names), and Gradio uses no private `httpx` internals, `httpcore`, or the newly deprecated `URL.raw`.
- **Requirements:** `httpx>=0.24.1(,<1.0)` → `httpx2>=2.0.0,<3.0` in both packages, and `safehttpx>=0.2.0,<0.3.0`.
- **`huggingface_hub` floor unchanged (>=1.16).** Hub 2.0 is the first release on `httpx2`, but the latest `transformers` (5.17) and `diffusers` (0.40) both cap `huggingface-hub<2.0`, so requiring it would make Gradio uninstallable alongside them. This doesn't need hub 2.0: Gradio never passes `httpx` objects to `huggingface_hub` or catches its exceptions. The one hub session call (`gradio skills`) catches a bare `Exception`.
- **`mcp` stays `<2.0` in this PR.** mcp 2.x is on `httpx2`, but moving to it means rewriting Gradio's MCP server, so it's in the stacked follow-up, gradio-app/gradio#13921. Until then the `mcp` extra still installs `httpx` for mcp's own use. Gradio only uses `httpx2.URL` in `mcp.py` and never shares objects with mcp.
- **Semgrep:** the SSRF rule `no-bare-httpx-url-fetch-ssrf` now matches `httpx2.get(...)` and the other request functions as well as `httpx.*`. Without this it would silently stop catching anything.
- **Test deps:** dropped `respx`, which isn't used anywhere and only mocks `httpx`. Recompiled `test/requirements.txt`: `httpx2==2.13.0` in, `respx` out. `httpx` stays as a transitive dependency of `diffusers`, `openai` and hub 1.x.
- `[tool.uv]` exempts `safehttpx` from the 7-day `exclude-newer` window, so the new 0.2.0 resolves in CI right away.

One behaviour change to be aware of: `httpx2` verifies TLS against the OS trust store (via `truststore`) instead of `certifi`'s bundle. `SSL_CERT_FILE`/`SSL_CERT_DIR` and `ssl_verify=False` still work as before.

### Verification
**CI is green** on this branch. The first run failed only because `safehttpx` 0.2.0 wasn't published yet. One `docs-build` job then resolved just minutes after the release, got a stale PyPI index, and passed on a re-run.

Locally, Python 3.10 venv, installed in CI's order:
```bash
python -m pytest -n 8 -m "not flaky" test                     # 1302 passed
cd client/python && python -m pytest -n 8 -m "not flaky" test/ # 171 passed
ruff check gradio test client && ruff format --check gradio test client && ty check  # clean
```
The only full-suite failures come from the local environment: 12 Docker reverse-proxy tests (no Docker daemon, bare `python` not on `PATH`) and `test_get_executable_path` (`uv venv` has no `pip`). `test_interfaces.py::test_close` failed once under `-n 8`, because it's a `serial` test that clashed on a port, and passes on its own. None of these involve HTTP clients.

Also checked by hand in clean venvs: no authlib warning with `huggingface_hub` 2.0 (no `httpx` installed at all) or with hub 1.33 (`httpx` present, authlib picks `httpx2`). The demo below renders, fetches the image server-side through `safehttpx`'s IP-pinned `httpx2` transport (following the Hub's CDN redirect), and the mocked login works. The demo file was not committed.

```python
import gradio as gr


def greet(profile: gr.OAuthProfile | None):
    if profile is None:
        return "You are not logged in."
    return f"Hello, {profile.name}!"


with gr.Blocks() as demo:
    gr.LoginButton()
    greeting = gr.Markdown()
    gr.Image("https://huggingface.co/datasets/huggingface/documentation-images/resolve/main/beignets-task-guide.png")
    demo.load(greet, None, greeting)

demo.launch()
```
