prs.title: Fix streaming gr.Audio getting stuck at "queue: 1/1" when stopped while waiting
prs.body:
## Description

Stopping a streaming microphone `gr.Audio` while the button shows "Waiting" left the output stuck at `queue: 1/1`, and the next Record stayed at "Waiting" until the page was reloaded. Clicking "Waiting" is meant to work like Stop (it cancels the recording before the server starts processing it), so this PR makes that cancel clean up properly instead of disabling the button. Two separate problems combined to cause the hang, and each one alone still breaks the next recording.

1. `close_stream()` in the JS client posted to `/stream/${event_id}/close` right away. While `/queue/join` is still in flight the event id is empty, so the request went to `/stream//close` and got a 404. The server event was never closed, kept waiting for chunks and held the function's concurrency slot. `close_stream()` now closes the iterator immediately and sends the close request once the join has returned the event id. `send_chunk()` had the same problem (a chunk sent in that window went to `/stream/` and was lost), so it gets the same treatment. Both wait on the same promise, so they are still sent in call order.

2. In `InteractiveAudio.svelte`, a chunk that passed the recording check was still uploading when Stop was clicked. When the upload finished, it was dispatched as a `stream` event. The submission had already been cleared by the close, so this opened a brand new stream that nothing ever closed, queued behind the event from (1). A chunk whose upload finishes after recording has stopped is now dropped. This race does not depend on which button is shown; it only needs an upload in flight at Stop, which is why the test clicks Stop rather than Waiting.

Known limitation: if the user stops and starts recording again before the stale chunk's upload finishes, that chunk is sent as the first chunk of the new recording. I kept the simple `recording` check rather than adding a per-recording counter, since the window is short and the effect is a fraction of a second of extra audio.

The microphone staying open after a Stop during "Waiting" is fixed separately in #13901. Both PRs add a `media_recorder` stub to `js/audio/audio.test.ts`, so whichever lands second needs a small merge there.

Closes: #13900

prs.title: Fetch channel data once per channel when encoding recorded audio to WAV
prs.body:
## Description

`audioBufferToWav` called `audioBuffer.getChannelData(channel)` inside the per-sample loop, so a single encode made `length * channels` calls. It runs every time a microphone recording is stopped and every time audio is trimmed (through `process_audio`). In most browsers each call is cheap, but @zen-ham measured that in Thorium 138 the cost of a call grows with the buffer length, so the encode becomes quadratic in clip length and the page freezes for seconds (11.4 s for a 3.24 s clip).

This fetches each channel's `Float32Array` once before the loop and indexes into it, which is the fix suggested in the issue. The output bytes are unchanged, and the number of `getChannelData` calls no longer depends on how a browser implements it. Thanks to @zen-ham for the report and the measurements.

To check this without an affected browser, I wrapped `AudioBuffer.prototype.getChannelData` with a 50 µs busy-wait and counted the calls. Recording about 6 s and pressing Stop took 301,684 calls on the release and 5 on this branch (the other calls come from process_audio and the waveform rendering), and the freeze went away.

Closes: #13898

prs.title: Release the microphone when a streaming gr.Audio recording is stopped
prs.body:
## Description

With `gr.Audio(sources=["microphone"], streaming=True)`, stopping a recording left the microphone in use until the page was closed.

`InteractiveAudio.svelte` opened the stream with `getUserMedia` in `prepare_audio()` and passed it to the streaming `MediaRecorder` without keeping a reference. `stop()` and `onDestroy` only called `recorder.stop()`, and stopping a `MediaRecorder` does not stop the tracks of the stream it records. The stream is now kept and its tracks are stopped in both places. `inited` is also reset so the next recording opens a fresh stream, which means each recording now gets its own recorder instance (the recorder constructor from #11970 is still created only once). I checked ten Record/Stop cycles in a row: output kept arriving and every stream was released.

Resetting `inited` exposed an existing double call: from the second recording on, `record()` runs once from the Record click and once from the `recording && recorder` effect. Before, the second call skipped `prepare_audio()` because `inited` was already true; now both calls would open a stream and one would leak. The two calls now share a single `prepare_audio()` promise. The same double call also fired `start_recording` twice per take (this predates the PR); each take is now announced once.

The same leak also happened when recording was stopped, or the component was unmounted, while `getUserMedia()` was still pending (for example with the permission prompt open): the stream that resolved afterwards was never stopped, and in the Stop case recording even started. `record()` now releases the stream in that case, and `stop()` no longer throws when no recorder exists yet. Because every take now requests the microphone again, a failed request (permission revoked, another app holding the mic, a headset unplugged) is more likely than before, so `record()` now leaves the recording state instead of restarting the previous recorder on its stopped tracks. Errors other than `NotAllowedError` used to be rethrown, which left the UI stuck on Stop; they are now reported with a generic message (`audio.recording_error`).

The waveform visualizer in `StreamAudio.svelte` opens its own microphone stream, which had two similar gaps. The "Waiting" button (shown between sending the stream request and the server starting to process it) called only `stop()`, while the Stop button calls `waveformRecord?.stopMic()` first, so stopping during that phase left that stream open. And the component never destroyed its WaveSurfer instance, so unmounting while recording left it open too. The Waiting button now calls `stopMic()`, and the waveform is destroyed on unmount, as `AudioRecorder` already does.

Switching the source to Upload while recording unmounted `StreamAudio` but left the stream and recorder in `InteractiveAudio` running, so chunks kept being sent. That also predates this PR, but it is the same symptom, so recording now stops when the source leaves the microphone.

Stopping during the "Waiting" phase also used to leave the output's status tracker stuck at `queue: 1/1`. That was a separate bug in the stream/queue handling (#13900), fixed in #13903.

Closes: #13897

prs.title: Block PRs that contain pre-rewrite history
prs.body:
## Description

Gradio's git history was rewritten to remove large files that were no longer in the repo (#9372); a fresh clone went from ~359 MiB to ~126 MiB. Any branch cut from `main` before the rewrite still carries the old history, and merging one would bring it back along with its large files. That is how a similar rewrite in October 2021 was undone.

This adds a `history-check` workflow whose `block-pre-rewrite-history` job fails any PR whose head contains a commit that exists only in the old history. It uses a commits-only partial clone, so it runs in seconds.

To block merges, `block-pre-rewrite-history` needs to be added as a required status check on `main` after this is merged.

Closes: #9372

prs.title: Prototype component tooltips for Textbox, Image, and FileExplorer
prs.body:
## Description **Draft / design prototype.** This PR prototypes a `tooltip=` parameter so we can settle on a frontend design before rolling it out to every component. It is wired up for three components only: `gr.Textbox` (label rendered by `BlockTitle`), plus `gr.Image` and `gr.FileExplorer` (label rendered as a `BlockLabel` chip). A new `Tooltip` atom in `@gradio/atoms` renders four candidate designs. You pick one with a **temporary** `?tooltip_design=` query parameter, which will be removed once a design is chosen: | `?tooltip_design=` | Design | Mobile / touch | Discoverable? | |---|---|---|---| | `icon` (default) | ⓘ button after the label. Hover or focus shows a popover; click pins it open | Tap toggles | Yes, the icon is always visible | | `underline` | Dotted underline on the label text (like ``). Hover or focus shows the popover | Tap toggles | Weak | | `hover` | No extra UI. Hovering or focusing anywhere in the component shows the popover above the label (closest to the original `title=` ask) | No | No | | `inline` | ⓘ button toggles an inline panel under the label. No popover | Tap toggles | Yes | This responds to the accessibility and mobile concerns in the issue thread. Designs `icon` and `inline` keep an always-visible affordance and work by tap. All popover designs: - open on keyboard focus and close on Escape - stay open while the pointer moves into the bubble (WCAG 1.4.13) - use `role="tooltip"` and `aria-describedby` The bubble renders in the top layer via the Popover API, so it isn't clipped by a block's `overflow: hidden`. Its colours invert automatically in dark mode. Backend plumbing is intentionally minimal. `Component.__init__` accepts `tooltip` (mirroring `info`), and only `Textbox`, `Image`, and `FileExplorer` expose it for now. Closes: #4278 ### Open questions for review - Which design (or combination, e.g. `icon` on desktop plus `inline` behaviour on touch)? - Should `tooltip` become a shared prop on every component, next to `label`/`info`? - What should happen when `show_label=False`? Right now the tooltip is hidden along with the label. ### Verification - Checked all four designs in a browser against the built frontend and the `pnpm dev` server: hover, click-to-pin, keyboard focus/Escape, dark mode, and the Image label chip over the upload area. - `pytest test/components/test_textbox.py test/components/test_image.py test/components/test_file_explorer.py` passes. Exact-config assertions were updated to include `"tooltip": None`. - `ruff` 0.12.9 check and format, prettier, and eslint are clean on the changed files. `svelte-check` reports no errors in them. - `vitest run js/textbox js/image js/fileexplorer js/atoms`: all pass except `js/imageeditor/shared/brush/brush-textures.test.ts`, which fails the same way without this change.
Demo (not committed) ```python from pathlib import Path import gradio as gr HERE = Path(__file__).parent SWITCHER = """
Tooltip design: A · Info icon + popover · B · Dotted-underline label · C · Hover anywhere on component · D · Icon toggles inline help
""" def generate(prompt, negative, image): text = f"Prompt: {prompt!r}\nNegative: {negative!r}" return text, image with gr.Blocks() as demo: gr.Markdown("# Component tooltips (prototype for #4278)") gr.HTML(SWITCHER) with gr.Row(): with gr.Column(): prompt = gr.Textbox( label="Prompt", placeholder="A photo of an astronaut riding a horse", tooltip="Describe what you want to see. More specific prompts give more predictable results.", ) negative = gr.Textbox( label="Negative prompt", info="Always-visible `info` text, for comparison.", tooltip="Things to steer the model **away** from, e.g. `blurry, low quality`.", ) gr.Textbox(label="Seed (no tooltip, for comparison)", value="42") image_in = gr.Image( label="Reference image", type="filepath", tooltip="Optional. The output keeps the composition of this image. Drop a file or click to upload.", ) btn = gr.Button("Generate", variant="primary") with gr.Column(): out_text = gr.Textbox( label="Result", lines=3, tooltip="Echo of the inputs that were sent to the model.", ) image_out = gr.Image( label="Output image", value=str(HERE / "test" / "test_files" / "bus.png"), interactive=False, tooltip="The generated image. Use the buttons in the corner to download or view it fullscreen.", ) gr.FileExplorer( label="Theme files", root_dir=HERE / "gradio" / "themes", glob="*.py", tooltip="Pick one or more theme source files. Folders expand when clicked.", ) btn.click(generate, [prompt, negative, image_in], [out_text, image_out]) if __name__ == "__main__": demo.launch() ``` The demo file lives at the repo root of the working copy and was not committed.

prs.title: Add an app view to gr.Workflow
prs.body:
https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/4b282f48-1022-411f-8caf-c75fbd97dff2



Every `gr.Workflow` now also renders as a standard Gradio app (the "app view"). Visitors without write access see the app by default: that covers non-owners on a Space and anyone opening a local app without the write-access link. People with write access land on the canvas. A rounded **App / Workflow** toggle in the bottom-left of both views switches between them.

**Why:** For most Spaces, a node canvas is not as easy to use as a a regular Gradio app unless you're building or tinkering with the flow. The app view gives visitors a normal Gradio app and keeps the workflow one click away.

**How:** It reuses what we already have. `WorkflowEndpointManager` already builds real Gradio input/output components and a click event for each output group's API endpoint. Until now they sat in a hidden column. They are now laid out visibly, the way `gr.Interface` does it: inputs and **Run** on the left, outputs on the right, and one tab per independent pipeline, like `TabbedInterface`. So the Run buttons *are* the API endpoints, and "Use via API" in the footer documents exactly what's on screen.

Backend (`gradio/workflow_api.py`, `gradio/workflow.py`):
- The layout is rendered into a static `#workflow-app` column. The `gr.LoginButton` (Spaces + OAuth) is moved in there and made visible.
- Inputs are pre-filled with the reference nodes' current values, which also makes those values the API parameters' defaults.
- A markdown output renders as `gr.Markdown`. A graph with no outputs shows an empty state. The page title is set to the workflow's name.
- Node failures are raised as `gr.Error`, so app users see the actual message instead of a generic "Error".
- Teardown now tracks every block and event created inside the render context, because the layout has nested containers.
- `sync()` skips the rebuild when the app/API shape is unchanged, so component and event ids stay stable across most saves.
- New `get_app_version` server function lets the frontend tell when its copy of the app is stale.

Frontend (`js/workflowcanvas`):
- Auth moves up from `WorkflowCanvas.svelte` into `Index.svelte`, which picks the view: the `?ui=app|canvas` param wins, otherwise the choice follows write access. Before the server answers, the view is guessed from the write-token cookie or URL.
- The canvas is mounted the first time it's shown and kept mounted afterwards.
- `#workflow-app` is made `inert` while the canvas covers it.
- The pagehide autosave only runs if the canvas was ever mounted; otherwise it would have saved the store's placeholder over the file.
- New `app_view` prop on `gr.WorkflowCanvas`. Standalone `gr.WorkflowCanvas` usage is unchanged.

prs.title: Support huggingface_hub 1.31 and 2.x
prs.body:
Gradio and gradio_client currently cap huggingface_hub below 2.0. Hub 2.0 replaces its HTTP backend with httpx2 and removes duplicate_space. The PR updates both packages to support Hub 1.31.x and 2.x, uses the Hub's HTTP compatibility import where appropriate, and replaces removed APIs.

Context: https://github.com/huggingface/huggingface_hub/issues/4802 and https://github.com/huggingface/huggingface_hub/releases/tag/v2.0.0

Closes https://github.com/gradio-app/gradio/issues/13890

**Note:** since gradio is itself using `safehttpx` which is only compatible with `httpx` and not `httpx2` (yet?), it means that both `httpx` and `httpx2` will be installed when installing `gradio` with `huggingface_hub 2.x`. This is not a problem in practice, though it'd be great to bump `safehttpx` (or to create a new `safehttpx2` package? and deprecate the base one?). Under the hood, all calls forwarded by gradio to huggingface_hub will use `httpx2`.

prs.title: Name rejected files in upload errors and fix a Document leak in sanitize
prs.body:
## Description

Two small fixes:

1. **Name the rejected files in upload validation errors (#13879).** `Upload` and `UploadButton` now report every rejected file in one error (listing up to 5 names, with directory-relative paths for directory uploads) instead of one generic toast per file, using a shared `invalid_file_type_message` helper.
2. **Fix a Document leak in frontend sanitization (#13884).** `amuchina` creates its node iterator on the main `document` while the root lives in the throwaway `DOMParser` document, so every `sanitize()` call (every Markdown/Chatbot render, and every streamed chunk) pinned a parsed document in memory. This adds a pnpm patch (`patches/amuchina@1.0.12.patch`) that creates the iterator on the root's own document, plus a regression test. Amuchina appears to be unmaintained (its last release and repository push were in April 2024), so we are carrying a local patch rather than waiting for an upstream fix.

The FileExplorer folder-selection changes for #11390 that were previously in this PR have been removed and will be handled separately.

prs.title: Preserve the alpha channel of images loaded into `gr.ImageEditor`
prs.body:
## Description

`gr.ImageEditor` flattened every image onto an opaque background, so an RGBA image came back to the handler with its transparent areas filled in white. Since #13787 an untouched editor re-uploads the original bytes, so a round trip with no editing happens to keep its alpha; the loss shows as soon as anything is edited, which is the point of using the component at all.

`LayerManager.create_background_layer()` painted an opaque rectangle into the background layer's own render texture, and the image sprite was then added as a child of that same container. `get_blobs()` extracts the background layer and the whole image container, so both the `background` and the `composite` that reach the backend were the image composited over that rectangle. The alpha channel was still there, it was just uniformly 255.

The fill itself is not wrong: on an empty canvas it is what makes the editor read as a sheet you can draw on. It only has no business being in the exported image when the layer is about to hold a background image. So `create_background_layer()` now takes a `transparent` flag, which the places that immediately put an image on the layer pass, and the flag is remembered on the `LayerManager` so the resize path keeps it. An empty canvas is unchanged and still exports an opaque background, which keeps `gr.Sketchpad` / `gr.Paint` apps that read `composite` working as before. The three outputs keep their existing division of labour: `background` is the image as loaded, `layers` are the strokes on their own, and `composite` is the layers over the background, so a stroke drawn across a transparent area is opaque in `composite`.

Once transparency survives, the editor has to show it, otherwise a transparent area and a white one look identical while you edit. The checkerboard behind the canvas is drawn whenever the background layer is transparent, at the same cell size as the colour picker's opacity slider. It is a sibling of the sheet rather than part of it, because the sheet carries a drop shadow generated from its own alpha and that would smear the pattern. It is kept in its own commits so it can be dropped without touching the data fix, if you would rather land that first, but its on/off condition is the state the data fix introduces, so they really are one change.

Two docstrings this issue exposed are fixed as well. `image_mode` still described `gr.Image`'s "RGB"/"L" options instead of this component's `"RGBA"` default, and `type="numpy"` claimed a shape of `(height, width, 3)` when the default image mode gives four channels.

Keeping the background transparent has a knock-on effect on image modes without an alpha channel. The canvas exports RGB 0 under alpha 0, and `convert_and_format_image()` converted with a plain `im.convert(image_mode)`, which drops alpha without compositing, so `image_mode="RGB"` would have started returning black where it used to return white. It now composites `background` and `composite` onto white before converting to a mode without alpha, so an edited image in RGB mode comes back exactly as before. This also removes an existing inconsistency: an untouched editor sends the original file (#13787), which in RGB mode came back with whatever RGB the PNG stores under its transparent pixels (black for most files), while an edited one came back white. Both are white now. Layers are left alone, since they are strokes read as masks and already came back black under transparency.

A transparent background also exposed how the canvas was exported. pixi reads pixels back premultiplied and, in the version we use, does not undo that on extract, so a semi-transparent pixel came back darker (a 50% white pixel as `[128, 128, 128, 128]`, and `[191, 191, 191]` once flattened in RGB mode). The opaque fill used to hide this. `get_canvas_blob()` now reads the pixels with `extract.pixels()`, divides the colour by alpha, and encodes the result, so that pixel comes back as `[255, 255, 255, 128]` (`[255, 255, 255]` in RGB mode). Every export goes through this function, so semi-transparent pixels in `layers` (antialiased stroke edges, strokes drawn with reduced opacity) now keep their colour too, where they used to come back darker.

One behaviour change worth flagging: in the default RGBA mode, when the image is smaller than a `fixed_canvas`, the padding around it is now transparent rather than white, and the checkerboard shows through there. That is what an outpainting workflow wants, but it is a change. In RGB mode the padding stays white. Handlers that take the default RGBA output and drop the alpha channel themselves (`x[..., :3]`, or PIL's `convert("RGB")`, which does not composite) used to get white in transparent areas and now get whatever RGB sits under them, so they should composite onto a background or switch to `image_mode="RGB"`. The `image_mode` docstring now says this. The RGB values under fully transparent pixels still differ between the two paths in RGBA mode (the file's own values when untouched, zero after an edit). The canvas cannot keep them, and rewriting untouched files to match would undo #13787, so I left that as is.

Closes: #11628

| `dataset` | 12 | 57 | `layout`, `sample_labels`, `headers`, pagination, example-component prop forwarding, `click`/`select`/`change`, `get_data`/`set_data` |
| `highlightedtext` | 26 (2 skipped) | 59 | Renamed `highlightedtext.test.ts` → `HighlightedText.test.ts`; both skips revived; adds `combine_adjacent`, `show_inline_category`, `show_whitespaces`, `buttons`, label, empty state, events, `get_data`/`set_data` |
| `imageeditor` | 10 | 56 | Static vs interactive mode, toolbar `sources`/`transforms`/brush/eraser, controls, layers; sub-components driven in isolation through the existing test wrapper |

`js/spa/test/components.test.ts` only asserted `elem_id` / `elem_classes` / `visible` / `label` across ~30 components, all of which `run_shared_prop_tests` now covers per component — except `File`, so this adds `run_shared_prop_tests` to `File.test.ts` first.

Two `data-testid`-style hooks were added so the tests could avoid `container.querySelector`: `data-testid="drag-handle"` on the handle Draggable creates imperatively, and passthrough props on `ImageEditorTestWrapper`.

## Test suite cleanup

- **Removed every `test.todo` placeholder** across `js/` — 126 of them in 30 files. The suite now only contains tests that actually run, so the summary line is a real signal rather than a mix of executed and deferred work. Six `describe` blocks that held nothing but todos were removed with them.
- **Removed six flaky tests** that failed intermittently under full-suite load: one in `audio.test.ts` (`skip_length affects skip button labels`), four in `Dataframe.test.ts` (`Enter activates the selected cell`, `F2 toggles edit mode`, `Tab moves between cells while editing`, `table with rows still fills the screen in fullscreen`), and one in `Tabs.test.ts` (`the tab overflow button has an accessible name`). All six predate this PR and all are load-sensitive races rather than real regressions — they pass in isolation and fail only when the whole suite runs in parallel.

## Bug fixes

The new tests surfaced five real defects. Each is fixed here with the test that covers it — happy to split these into a separate PR if you'd rather keep this one test-only.

1. **`js/nativeplot/Index.svelte`** — a list `sort` reached vega-embed as a `$state` proxy, which `structuredClone` rejects with `DataCloneError`, so `gr.BarPlot(..., sort=["b", "a"])` rendered **no chart at all**. Copied out of the proxy, matching the adjacent `[...colors_in_legend]`.
2. **`js/highlightedtext/Index.svelte`** — `StatusTracker` was given `onclearstatus`, but its prop is `on_clear_status`, so `gr.HighlightedText` never dispatched `clear_status` and the clear button on an errored status did nothing.
3. **`js/imageeditor/shared/resize/resize.ts`** — unmounting an ImageEditor threw `TypeError: Cannot read properties of null (reading 'canvas')`. Pixi's `canvas` getter dereferences a null renderer once the app is destroyed, so `?.app?.canvas` is not enough.
4. **`js/nativeplot/Index.svelte`** — clearing a plot's value while vega-embed was still resolving threw, because `chart_element` is unbound by then and `ResizeObserver.observe` rejects `undefined`.
5. **`js/highlightedtext/Index.svelte`** — an edit dispatched `change` **twice** (the `onchange` handler assigned `gradio.props.value` and dispatched, then the `$effect` watching `old_value` saw the same assignment and dispatched again), while a value pushed from the server dispatched once. The assignment alone is enough, so the explicit dispatch is removed and both paths now fire exactly once.

prs.title: Stop converting .m4b audio that browsers can already play
prs.body:
Fixes #13856

## Root cause

`.m4b` is the same mp4/ISO-BMFF container as `.m4a`, just under an audiobook name, and `route_utils.MEDIA_MIMETYPE_OVERRIDES` already serves it as `audio/mp4`. But `processing_utils.PLAYABLE_AUDIO_CODECS` listed only `.m4a` and `.mp4`, so `audio_is_playable()` returned `False` for every `.m4b`. `gr.Audio.postprocess` therefore warned *"Audio does not have browser-compatible container or codec"*, remuxed the stream into a full-size `.m4a` copy in the Gradio cache, and served that renamed file. The two tables disagreed; that disagreement is the bug.

The reporter describes a conversion to wav. On current `main` it is a lossless remux to `.m4a` rather than a wav re-encode (the remux path landed in #13728), so the audio does still play — but for an audiobook it means a needless duplicate of a large file on disk, a renamed download, and a warning that is untrue.

## What changes

- `processing_utils.PLAYABLE_AUDIO_CODECS` gains `(".m4b", "aac")`, mirroring the `.m4a` entry, so an AAC `.m4b` is served as-is.
- The pre-existing `(".m4a", "alac")` entry and the `"alac": ".m4a"` remux target are removed. Only Safari decodes ALAC, so serving an ALAC file unconverted (or remuxing an ALAC stream into `.m4a`) fails silently in Chrome and Firefox. ALAC now takes the wav re-encode path like any other undecodable codec.
- `gr.Audio.postprocess` no longer warns *"Converting to wav."*, which has been untrue for every remux since #13728. It now warns after converting and names the actual output suffix (e.g. *"Converted to .m4a."*), or says the conversion failed and the original is being served.
- The existing `test_audio_is_playable` covers `.m4b`, pinning the probed codec first so the assertion cannot pass through the "ffprobe failed, assume playable" fallback.

## I verified the browser-support claim rather than taking it on faith

The issue asserts that modern browsers can play `.m4b`. MDN's [container guide](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/Media/Guides/Formats/Containers) only documents `audio/mp4` with `.mp4`/`.m4a`, so I measured it: a local server served each file with exactly the `Content-Type` Gradio sends, and a page probed it with an `<audio>` element (`canPlayType`, `loadedmetadata`, `readyState`, real playback) plus `AudioContext.decodeAudioData`, the call wavesurfer uses to draw the waveform. One case per page load, Chrome run with `--autoplay-policy=no-user-gesture-required`.

| file served | Content-Type | Chrome 152 | Firefox 156 | Safari 26 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `.m4a`, AAC (control) | `audio/mp4` | plays, decodes | plays, decodes | plays, decodes |
| **`.m4b`, AAC** | `audio/mp4` | **plays, decodes** | **plays, decodes** | **plays, decodes** |
| `.m4b`, AAC, `M4B ` ftyp brand | `audio/mp4` | plays, decodes | plays, decodes | plays, decodes |
| `.m4b`, AAC | `application/octet-stream` | plays | plays | **fails, MEDIA_ERR_SRC_NOT_SUPPORTED** |

The claim holds: identical bytes behave identically whether named `.m4a` or `.m4b`, and the `M4B ` major brand changes nothing. The last row is why this fix is safe on its own — Safari refuses `octet-stream`, and Gradio already sends `audio/mp4` for `.m4b`.

## On the `.mov` half of the issue

Not included, deliberately. All three engines did play AAC in a QuickTime container served as `video/quicktime` (contradicting MDN, which lists QuickTime as "Only older versions of Safari" with `No` for every codec), but:

- Safari's `decodeAudioData` **fails** on `.mov` (`EncodingError`), so the waveform would break and fall back to the native player.
- `.mov` is overwhelmingly a video container. Treating it as playable audio would hand an `<audio>` element a file whose video track it cannot use, and stream the whole thing to play its audio. The current remux to `.m4a` drops the video track and is the better outcome.
- `.mov` is not in `video_is_playable` either, so admitting it only to the audio allowlist would be inconsistent.

Happy to revisit if maintainers disagree.

## Verification

```bash
pytest test/test_processing_utils.py -q      # 70 passed
pytest test/components/test_audio.py -q      # 21 passed
ruff check / ruff format --check gradio/processing_utils.py gradio/components/audio.py test/test_processing_utils.py
```

Before: `gr.Audio` serves `chapter-01.m4a` (a cache copy) and warns. After: serves the original `chapter-01.m4b` as `audio/mp4`, no warning, no copy. Confirmed playing with a rendered waveform in the browser.

## Minimal demo (not committed)

```python
import gradio as gr

with gr.Blocks() as demo:
    gr.Markdown("## My audiobook")
    gr.Audio("audiobook/chapter-01.m4b", label="Chapter 1")
    gr.Audio("audiobook/chapter-02.m4b", label="Chapter 2")

demo.launch()
```

Chapters generated with `ffmpeg -f lavfi -i "sine=frequency=380:duration=90" -c:a aac -b:a 64k chapter-01.m4b`. Click the download icon: before the fix the file arrives as `.m4a`, after it keeps its `.m4b` name.

prs.title: Clear the loading status when a validator rejects an event
prs.body:
## Description

When an event's `validator=` rejects a call, the frontend paints the rejection onto the components directly and returns early from the submit loop. That early return skips the loading-status bookkeeping that every other terminal branch of the loop performs, so the run's entry in `LoadingStatusState.current` stays `pending`, timestamp and all.

Nothing looks wrong yet, because the rejection path also writes `status: null` straight onto the output components. But the next event dispatched anywhere in the app calls `update_loading_stati_state()`, which re-applies every entry of `current` to its component. The stale `pending` entry is repainted with its original `time_start`, so a spinner appears on the rejected event's output and counts up from where the rejected run would have been. It clears only when that event is later run successfully, or on a page reload.

The fix settles the status the same way the other terminal branches do, with `update_loading_status({ status: "complete" })`, and leaves the manual component painting in place so the validation errors just written to the inputs are not clobbered.

Three details worth calling out for review:

`"complete"` rather than `"error"`: `StatusTracker` hides itself for `complete` exactly as it does for a null status, while `error` renders an error state, which is not what a validation rejection should show on an output. It also matches the connection-lost branch, which uses `complete` for the same "the function never ran" case. Settling the status also fixes the screen-reader announcer from #13861, where `previous_statuses` used to stay on `pending` for the rejected event, so the next real run of it never announced "Loading" again. So that a refused run is not announced as "Complete", the settle carries the invalid inputs' messages as `validation_error` and `LiveStatus` reads those instead. It does this even when `show_progress` is hidden, since the error is shown on the inputs either way. `LoadingStatusState` does not store the field, so it is never repainted onto the progress targets.

The manual clear loop now iterates the components the loading status was actually registered against. That is `show_progress_on || outputs`, so when an event sets `show_progress_on` the clear was previously writing to components that never had a loading status and missing the one that did. Since the same expression was already spelled out by hand in two other places, and this bug is what happens when those copies drift, it is now `Dependency.progress_targets` and all three sites go through it.

Streaming events need the settle to close the stream. `resolve_args` only counts an input component as part of an event's loading status while `stream_state` is set, so settling with `stream_state: null` left a stream dependency's input rows untouched and #13869 survived there. Passing the `stream_state` already in scope brings them in, and closing the stream is what actually unsticks them, because `Webcam` and `InteractiveAudio` decide whether to drop incoming chunks from `stream_state` alone without looking at the status. It is guarded on `connection_type`: the complete branch sets `"closed"` unconditionally, but doing that here would pull inputs into the loading status for ordinary events too, and the next repaint would then wipe the validation errors this branch has just written to them.

Closes: #13869

prs.title: Stop validators from overwriting their own inputs
prs.body:
## Description

`create_validator_fn` builds the validator's `BlockFunction` with `outputs=fn.inputs`, so every value a validator returns was run through `postprocess_data` as if it were a new value for the input it judged. Three things followed from that:

- A `gr.State` in the event's `inputs=` ended up holding the `gr.validate()` dict itself. Other components get a fresh value from the client on the next call, so they recover; a `gr.State` never does, so it stays corrupted for the rest of the session.
- An invalid verdict on a `gr.State` never blocked the call. The stateful branch of `postprocess_data` appends `None` to the output list, so `process_validation_response` saw a non-dict for that slot and substituted `{"is_valid": True}`. The same validator on a `Textbox` rejected the call correctly.
- For non-stateful inputs the verdict dict was written into the session's tracked config values. That is normally invisible, because the real handler immediately rewrites them from the request payload, but when validation fails the handler never runs, so the dict sticks. It is observable through `gr.DeepLinkButton`: a link generated after a rejected call restores `{'__type__': 'validate', ...}` into the input instead of its real value.

The fix marks the synthetic validator function with `is_validator_function` and has `postprocess_data` return its values untouched. A verdict is not a component output, so it should neither update session state nor be postprocessed, and the guard sits above the per-output loop because for a validator that loop had become a copy. Everything before it (`validate_outputs`, the single-value and dict normalizations, `skip()` expansion) is unchanged, so nothing that reaches that point today reaches it differently.

I went with the flag rather than keeping validators off this path altogether. `Queue.push` could run `preprocess_data` and `call_function` itself and hand `result["prediction"]` straight to `process_validation_response`, which is what `test_validator_receives_the_same_keyword_inputs` already does, and then verdicts would never enter the output machinery at all. That is the better shape, but it means reimplementing the session restore, OAuth token and root path handling that `call_process_api` gives us today, which is more than this bug needs.

The flag is deliberately specific to the validator rather than keying off `postprocess=False`, since ordinary handlers with `postprocess=False` legitimately write to a `gr.State`.

Two dead stores in `Queue.push` go with it, both spotted while reading that method for the validator path. The `Event` built for the validator function is shadowed by the real event below before anything reads it, so it reads as if the validator run were queued and tracked when it is not; that one belongs to this work. The session lookup at the top is ordinary dead code that happens to sit in the same method: it resolves `fn` and is overwritten two lines later by `route_utils.get_fn`, which branches on `body.session_hash` and indexes the same mapping. It is not a pure read, since `StateHolder.__getitem__` creates the `SessionState` when it is missing and touches the LRU, but `get_fn` does that too, so removing the first copy changes nothing.

One consequence worth flagging: now that an invalid verdict on a `gr.State` blocks the call, the rejection has no visible representation in the UI, because a `gr.State` has no component to paint the message onto. It does surface over the API. So an app whose validator already returns `gr.validate(False, ...)` for a `gr.State` slot goes from silently ignoring that verdict, while corrupting the state, to silently refusing the call. Both are bad in their own way and the second is at least honest about the verdict, but it is a change of behaviour on upgrade rather than a pure fix, and whether the message should also reach a toast is worth a maintainer's call.

Closes: #13855

- [After fix](https://huggingface.co/spaces/hysts-debug/gradio-13855-after) (the wheel built for this PR)

Both apps carry a note about it, but to save you the surprise: once any validator on either page rejects a call, the next click anywhere leaves a spinner running forever on that event's output box. That is #13869, a separate frontend bug this PR does not touch, and it happens on both Spaces. Reload to clear it.

prs.title: Fix deep links on Windows
prs.body:
Fixes the one genuine code failure in the checks on https://github.com/gradio-app/gradio/pull/13853: `test/test_routes.py::TestRoutes::test_multipage_config_and_info_can_be_scoped_to_page` failing with `KeyError: 'components'` on `test-windows-latest-not-flaky`.

## The bug

`load_deep_link` in [gradio/routes.py](gradio/routes.py) built the `state.json` lookup with `Path`:

```python
user_path = Path("deep_links") / deep_link / "state.json"
path = Path(routes_safe_join(DeveloperPath(app.uploaded_file_dir), UserProvidedPath(str(user_path))))
```

On Windows that string is `deep_links\<id>\state.json`. `utils.safe_join` rejects any path containing the OS separator, so `routes_safe_join` raised `HTTPException(403)` for **every** deep link. `load_deep_link` caught only `FileNotFoundError`, `OSError` and `orjson.JSONDecodeError`, so the exception escaped and `GET /config?deep_link=...` returned an error body instead of a config — hence the `KeyError: 'components'` in the test.

Deep links were therefore broken on Windows in general, not just under test. It went unnoticed because the one test that covered them end to end, `test_deep_link_unique_per_session`, is `skipif(sys.platform == "win32")`; the new test added in #13843 reaches the same code through `TestClient`, which needs no port, and so exposed it.

A second bug sits in the same function: `routes_safe_join` raises `HTTPException(404)` when the path does not exist, which made the `else: deep_link_state = "invalid"` branch unreachable. A stale or bogus deep link failed the whole `/config` request rather than reporting an invalid link, even though both frontends handle `deep_link_state === "invalid"` by showing a toast over an otherwise working app.

## The fix

- Build the relative path with forward slashes so it survives `safe_join` on every platform. Traversal is still rejected: `../escaping` normalises to `../escaping/state.json` and raises as before.
- Catch `HTTPException` as well, and fall back to the components the app would normally load, so an unusable deep link degrades to `deep_link_state: "invalid"` with a working app instead of an error response.

## Tests

- `test_deep_link_is_read_with_an_os_independent_path` — a valid deep link resolves through `/config`. Passes everywhere; fails on Windows without the fix.
- `test_unusable_deep_link_falls_back_to_the_default_config` — a missing link and a traversal attempt both return 200 with `deep_link_state == "invalid"` and the full component set. Both fail on every platform without the fix.

`test_routes.py` locally: 181 passed against a 178-passed baseline on `main`, with the same 16 pre-existing failures in both runs (unrelated local environment gaps, not touched by this change).

## Not addressed here

The other red checks on #13853 are infrastructure, not code:

- `test-ubuntu-latest-flaky` / `test-windows-latest-flaky` — all 9 failures are `401 Client Error` against `huggingface.co`; the `HF_TOKEN` secret looks expired.
- `npm-previews` — pkg.pr.new returned `404 {"message":"There is no workflow defined for Bd9Cc07URK"}`.
- `test_server_launch_enables_mcp` on Windows — `Cannot find empty port in range: 7860-7959`; port exhaustion across `pytest-xdist` workers.

All four of these jobs are `continue-on-error` in [test-python.yml](.github/workflows/test-python.yml), so they do not block #13853.

prs.title: Pass HF_TOKEN to the python workflow as a secret, not a variable
prs.body:
## Description

GitHub Actions masks values that come from `secrets.*` in job logs. It does **not** mask `vars.*` — repository variables are treated as configuration rather than credentials, so they are printed verbatim wherever a step dumps its environment.

`.github/workflows/test-python.yml` took its `HF_TOKEN` from `vars.HF_TOKEN`. That put the token in cleartext in the env block of every step of every job in the `python` workflow — it is plainly visible in, for example, the `Typecheck` step of the `build` job. This repository is public, so those logs are readable by anyone, and have been for as long as the line has existed.

This changes the one line to `secrets.HF_TOKEN`.

It was the only `vars.*` reference under `.github/` (`grep -rn '\${{ *vars\.' .github/`). The two other workflows that set an `HF_TOKEN` already do it correctly, from `secrets.HF_DOCS_TOKEN` and `secrets.PYPI_PREVIEWS_TOKEN`.

### Action needed alongside this

The exposed token (named `gradio-ci-test-repo-read`, a read-scoped token) has been **revoked**, and the `HF_TOKEN` repository variable has been **deleted**. So on `main` today this line already resolves to nothing.

Merging this alone does not restore the workflow's access. A repository **secret** named `HF_TOKEN`, holding a fresh token with the same read scope, needs to exist. Until it does, `HF_TOKEN` will be empty in CI and the tests in `test/test_external.py` that reach Hugging Face through `huggingface_hub.get_token()` will run unauthenticated.

Rotating rather than reusing the old token is the point: it was public, so it had to be replaced regardless of how it is wired in.

### Why there is no linked issue

`AGENTS.md` asks for an issue before a PR unless the fix is very small. This is a one-line change, and writing the details up in a public issue before the wiring is fixed would have drawn attention to a live credential. The token is revoked now, which is why this description can be specific.

prs.title: Expose live Model3D camera and ImageSlider divider position to event handlers
prs.body:
Makes `camera_position` on `gr.Model3D` and `slider_position` on `gr.ImageSlider` follow the user, so a function whose parameter is annotated with the component reads the view that is actually on screen. Both can still be set from the backend to move the camera or the divider.

`gr.Model3D` updates `camera_position` as the Babylon camera moves. The observer is registered once and cleaned up with the component. `gr.ImageSlider` reports drags of the divider through a callback fired only on user input, so a position arriving as a prop can never echo back.


https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/eb715ad6-c4f5-462d-b0cd-ed9678b39804



Closes: #10128

### Also fixed in the same area

- `camera_position` is applied on load for `display_mode="point_cloud"` and `"wireframe"`, not only `"solid"`.
- `camera_position` is applied to interactive (uploadable) `gr.Model3D`, and `slider_position` to interactive `gr.ImageSlider`. Both previously ignored it — and for `gr.ImageSlider` the upload path hardcoded `position={0.5}`.
- `pan_speed` is passed through to the `gr.Model3D` viewer; it was silently stuck at its default.
- A camera observer was added on every `update_camera()` call without ever being removed. Exactly one is now registered.
- A `camera_position` update arriving while a model was still loading could leak the previous model's camera. Replaced the ready flag with a load generation counter.

### Known limitation

Babylon clamps `radius` to an `upperRadiusLimit` derived from model size, so asking for `400` on a small model reports the clamped `~13.96`. This reproduces on a plain initial load and is the viewer's own limit, not the round trip. Previously the prop kept claiming `400` while the camera sat at `13.96`; it now reports the truth.

## Docs

The component-props feature (#12267) shipped with a demo and no guide coverage. This PR adds an **Accessing Component Properties** section to *More Blocks Features*, after *Gathering Event Data*, and a new `demo/model3d_camera_position` example: you orbit the model until it looks right and the app hands back the `camera_position` to paste into your own code, with a reset button showing the property works in both directions. The section also notes that the annotation must be a component class rather than a layout (`gr.Accordion` and friends silently do nothing), and points at `slider_position`, `selected_index` and `playback_position`.

## AI Disclosure

- [x] I used AI to investigate the issue, implement the fix and regression tests, run verification, and draft this description. I reviewed every changed line and manually verified the behavior in a browser.
- [ ] I did not use AI

## 🎯 PRs Should Target Issues

This PR targets #10128. I checked open PRs for duplicate Model3D camera work before starting and found none.

## Testing and Formatting Your Code

- `python3 -m ruff check` / `format` on all changed Python files
- Prettier and ESLint on all changed Svelte/TypeScript files
- `env PYTHONPATH=client/python:. python3 -m pytest test/test_component_props.py test/components/test_model3d.py -q` (7 passed)
- `pnpm exec vitest run --dir js/model3D` (86 passed, 8 todo) and `--dir js/imageslider` (65 passed, 8 todo)
- `pnpm exec playwright test js/spa/test/component_props.spec.ts --project=chrome` (1 passed)
- `pnpm --filter @self/spa build --emptyOutDir`

The browser test asserts the reported position is **exactly** the configured tuple rather than merely that it changed. I confirmed both halves are real regression tests: reverting only `js/model3D` and rebuilding fails with `29.999999999999996` / `"static_exact": false`, and reverting only `js/imageslider` fails with `"exact": true` after a drag.

`pnpm ts:check` reports no diagnostics in the changed files; the pre-existing errors in unrelated files remain.

## Description

Adds complementary controls for tab overflow and per-tab alignment:

- `gr.Tabs(overflow_behavior="menu" | "wrap")` selects the existing overflow menu or a multi-row tab bar. `"menu"` remains the default.
- `gr.Tab(alignment="left" | "right")` places a tab in the main group or a right-aligned utility group. `"left"` remains the default.
- `gr.TabbedInterface(..., tabs_kwargs={...})` passes layout options such as `overflow_behavior="wrap"` to its internal `gr.Tabs`.

The behaviors work together in both modes. Menu mode keeps the first and selected tabs visible before allocating space to right-aligned tabs, preserves utility-tab order, and immediately promotes a newly selected overflow tab. Wrap mode keeps every tab visible, constrains long labels to the available width, and uses subtle separators between rows while retaining the standard bottom baseline.

Both Python constructors now reject invalid `overflow_behavior` and `alignment` values with a `ValueError`. The overflow layout also responds explicitly when `overflow_behavior` changes at runtime.

Closes: #9853

prs.title: Move CI off an ffmpeg that dies reading MPEG-TS
prs.body:
## Description

The static ffmpeg 7.0.2 build `.github/actions/install-all-deps` pins exits with SIGSEGV on the runners as soon as it is handed an MPEG-TS file, whether that is ffprobe reading a `.ts` the segment muxer has just written or ffmpeg decoding one. Nothing in the suite has ever read one, so it has gone unnoticed: the only test that touches a `.ts` writes the bytes `transport-stream-bytes` into it and patches `get_video_duration_ffprobe` out.

It is the machine rather than the bytes or the pin's integrity. The binary CI runs hashes the same as a clean download; that same download reads the same files on an Ubuntu 22.04 box, under the full suite in parallel and again pinned to four cores; the crash survives `-cpuflags 0`, so it is not a SIMD path; and it happens on both runner CPUs seen so far, an AMD EPYC 7763 and an AMD EPYC 9V74.

So both platforms move to 8.1.2. A local run cannot show that this helps, since 7.0.2 passes locally too, and every workflow takes this action from `@main`, so the new pin cannot reach CI from a branch either. The question went to a runner directly instead, on a temporary step that fetched both builds and put the reproduction from #13848 to each. On an EPYC 7763:

```
ffmpeg version 7.0.2-static https://johnvansickle.com/ffmpeg/
PROBE 7.0.2: mux=0 ffprobe=139 decode=139
ffmpeg version n8.1.2-50-g1a748fe2cd-20260831
PROBE 8.1.2: mux=0 ffprobe=0 decode=0
```

Writing the `.ts` is fine on either, both reads segfault on 7.0.2 (139 being 128 + SIGSEGV), and 8.1.2 survives them. 9.0.1 was tried as well and is not the version to take: it fails `TestAudioPlayability::test_convert_audio_remuxes_already_playable_codec`, which asserts an AAC stream survives a remux byte for byte, and 8.1.2 passes it.

Both archives are served from a bucket rather than their upstream release. The Linux build has to come from BtbN, since johnvansickle has published nothing since 7.0.2, and BtbN releases one build a day and keeps only the last 14. The daily tag this PR first pinned had about ten days left, and it would not have failed at a predictable moment: the Actions cache would have covered the dead URL until the first miss. Their month-end builds are kept for two years and carry the same 8.1.2, but two years is a deadline rather than an answer, so `gradio/ci-deps` holds a copy of each archive instead, byte for byte what upstream serves, at paths that are never rewritten, public so fork PRs need no credentials.

Beside them, `provenance.json` records each original URL, upstream project, build commit and hash, `licenses/` carries the license files out of the archives, and `source/` carries BtbN's build recipe at the commit that produced the Linux archive. Neither BtbN nor GyanD ships source alongside its binaries; both identify theirs by commit, and that recipe does the same for every statically linked component, since each of its 86 package scripts pins its own repository and commit.

The pin also moves into a single step. It used to be spread across the cache key and the two download steps, which is why the key carried a hand-maintained `-v1` suffix; the archive hash now stands in for it, and changing a pin invalidates the cache on its own.

This is split out of #13847 rather than carried in it, because every workflow takes this action from `@main`, so the change does nothing for any PR until it is merged. #13847 adds the tests that first reach the crash, and skips them while the decoder cannot read MPEG-TS; they start running again on their own once this lands.

Closes: #13848

prs.title: Encode streamed video's audio once per stream
prs.body:
## Description

`gr.Video(streaming=True)` ran every yielded chunk through its own ffmpeg, re-encoding it into a `.ts`. Each chunk's AAC therefore came from a fresh encoder and opened with a priming frame that had no overlap-add partner, so the audio broke at every chunk boundary. That is #11733's defect in the video component, which #13820 fixed for `gr.Audio`. The playlist then wrote `#EXT-X-DISCONTINUITY` after every segment, because each one started at the muxer's own zero, so a player was told to reset its clock at every boundary and threw away what continuity there was.

The audio now goes through one `AacStreamEncoder` for the whole stream, the shape #13820 gave `gr.Audio`, and the video is copied rather than re-encoded. Per chunk that is an ffprobe, a decode of the audio, and a mux of copied video with copied ADTS onto a continuous timeline, so nothing is encoded except the audio, once. Chunks that are not H.264 still go through libx264, as every chunk used to, so anything that played before still plays.

That also answers the other half of the issue, though not in the way the first draft of this claimed. The old path's cost was never flat: it re-encoded the video, so it scaled with the frame. Both paths, 0.25 s chunks at 15 fps, mean over twenty of them on one machine:

| frame | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| 320x240 | 32.5 ms | 44.3 ms |
| 640x480 | 44.7 ms | 45.2 ms |
| 1280x720 | 65.7 ms | 48.2 ms |
| 1920x1080 | 100.8 ms | 53.2 ms |

So this is slower on a small frame, where an ffprobe and a decode cost more than re-encoding 320x240 does, and the gain arrives with the resolution: a chunk now costs about what it costs to decode its audio, whatever the picture is, where before 1080p cost three times what 240p did. It is three subprocesses a chunk against the old two, plus the one encoder that lives for the stream; what is saved is the encoding, not the spawning.

Measuring this needed chunks whose audio was not already damaged. Both realistic ways of producing them lose audio before gradio sees it: `-c copy` splitting cuts mid-AAC and writes each piece an edit list that skips real samples, and per-chunk AAC encoding gives every piece its own encoder edges. Chunks carrying ALAC decode back to their source sample for sample, so they measure this code and nothing else. On 8 s of continuous tone in 32 such chunks:

| | decoded | gaps | silence |
|---|---|---|---|
| chunks as handed over | 8.000 s | 0 | 0.00% |
| before | 8.916 s | 33 | 8.49% |
| after | 8.034 s | 2 | **0.36%** |

The two remaining gaps are at 0.000 s and 8.023 s: the stream's own start and end, none at a chunk boundary. That is what one encoder per stream is meant to look like, and `test_streamed_video_adds_no_silence_of_its_own` asserts it against the same maker at a shorter length. These chunks are a whole number of frames apiece, so the silence described below is not in them; a stream whose chunks are not still pays that at every boundary, which is the two tracks disagreeing rather than the encoder edge this removes.

Four things about the new path are not obvious from the diff:

- A one-frame ADTS input silently loses its `-itsoffset`, and the first segment usually is one frame, so the offset is applied at the muxer instead, after probing.
- The first segment's audio is topped up one AAC frame at a time rather than by a fixed four-frame lookahead. How many frames the encoder holds back is a property of the build and the rate - four at 44.1 and 48 kHz, two at 8, 16 and 22.05 - but what a frame costs is seconds, and one at 8 kHz is 128 ms against 23 ms at 44.1. Feeding the largest count at every rate put 256 ms of silence onto a 16 kHz stream that wanted 128, which is past the lead tolerance, so the chunk after it snapped the video clock and the opening picture froze for as long as the padding: on a generator yielding one frame at a time at 30 fps and 16 kHz, 0.26 s frozen and 0.996 s of timeline for 0.4 s of supplied video. Topping up until a frame comes out finds the count instead, and the lead tolerance is never less than two frames of the rate in hand, since a fixed tenth of a second is under one AAC frame at 8 kHz. Same reproduction after: the opening step is a frame and the timeline is 0.837 s.
- Every segment pins its MPEG-TS stream ids and continues the per-PID continuity counters, because each is muxed by its own ffmpeg and would otherwise restart them. ffmpeg read that as packet loss, reporting 44 `Packet corrupt` warnings over twelve seconds and dropping the packets, and the audio-only segment the flush produces took the id the others give H.264 and was discarded whole, losing a third of a second off the end of every stream.
- The audio is topped up with silence to wherever the video has reached, so what a chunk's own two tracks disagree about lands once, at that chunk's boundary, instead of accumulating. A chunk asking for 0.25 s at 15 fps carries four frames, which is 16.7 ms more video than audio, and 16.7 ms is what the padding then comes to; #11733 reported 36 ms in the same place. Letting the audio set the pace instead removes it, and puts two video frames on the same DTS about once a chunk, which `test_streamed_video_is_one_continuous_stream` catches. A chunk whose audio outlasts its video is the other way round, and trimming the audio would put back the gap this removes, so the audio is left where it falls until it leads by the lead tolerance - a tenth of a second, or two AAC frames of the rate in hand where that is longer, which it is below about 20 kHz; then the next chunk's video is placed where the audio has reached, and the playlist reports the move. That case is ordinary: a generator told to stop at its shorter track (`-shortest`) gets 0.2 s of video against 0.25 s of audio on ffmpeg 7 and later, and without this the sound was 2.2 s ahead of the picture after ten seconds of stream.

  **That move is a cadence, not a one-off, and it is worth being plain about.** On a generator whose *every* chunk overruns, the lead rebuilds after each correction and is paid off again at a fixed rhythm. On the `overrun_chunks` fixture in the tests - 24 chunks of 0.2 s of video against 0.25 s of audio - the picture holds still for 0.18 s eleven times, once every sixth frame, and 4.8 s of supplied video is served across a 5.95 s timeline, a fifth of it frozen. Held picture is the lesser of the two evils here: the alternatives are the sound walking 2.2 s ahead of it, or trimming audio back into the very gaps this PR removes. But it is a visible hitch on a common generator shape, it is not something that happens once, and an earlier draft of this description implied otherwise. Anyone reviewing the trade should know they are choosing periodic held frames, not a single correction at the start. hls.js closes the gap by starting the next segment's first frame where the last one ended and holding it for the difference, read back from what it hands MediaSource, and a `-c copy` split's own jitter, up to 46 ms measured, stays under the tolerance, so those streams come out byte for byte as they did. A chunk that carries no audio stream at all is topped up for the whole of its video rather than only the distance behind, so a stream that falls silent part-way keeps its audio track and the two clocks stay level. hls.js fixes its tracks on the first segment and will not take one that loses the audio half-way, and the flush segment is placed by the audio clock, which had been left 0.9 s behind the video it was billed to follow.
- The frames are placed one AAC frame early, to cancel the encoder's own delay. That delay is exactly one frame at every sample rate measured, 23 ms at 44.1 kHz and 64 ms at 16 kHz, and mp4 records it in an edit list where MPEG-TS has nowhere to put it.

`_EncoderSlot` and `_segment_from_frames` move to `gradio/audio_stream_encoder.py` so both components share them, unchanged apart from the names. `Video.get_video_duration_ffprobe` and `Video.async_convert_mp4_to_ts` are gone, and `.ts` chunks are no longer passed through untouched, since a chunk that keeps its own timeline breaks the continuity the playlist now promises.

### The player stall this turned up

Verifying the above in a browser was impossible at first, because playback froze a few seconds in while the loader ran on to the end of the stream. That turned out to predate this work and to be worse without it: patching the old `stream_output` back in froze the playhead at 0.209 s with the audio buffer stuck on a single fragment, which is the symptom #11273 was filed for.

hls.js's own log says why: `Playback stalling due to low buffer`. A generator slower than real time drains the buffer and playback stalls, and any model doing inference per chunk is slower than real time, so that much is unavoidable. It then never restarted: once the playhead freezes, the buffer ahead of it grows past `maxBufferLength`, hls.js stops loading, and nothing prods the element even though the data it was waiting for has arrived. The fragmented mp4 handed to the decoder was contiguous in both tracks with a second of it sitting past the playhead.

So `js/utils/src/hls.ts` keeps four seconds of buffer rather than one, and watches for a frozen playhead with a quarter second to spare and nudges it. hls.js nudges across a hole in the buffer but not across the end of one. Together they carry a 20 s stream supplied at a third of real time to its end; the buffer change alone only moves the freeze from 2 s to 13 s, since a buffer of any size drains eventually at that rate.

### A known limit: very short chunks leave a segment without audio

The encoder emits AAC frames in bursts, so a chunk carrying less audio than a burst completes no frame of its own and its segment goes out with a video track and no audio one. The audio is not lost, it is held and served with a later segment. At 44.1 kHz, 250 ms chunks never reach this, 66.7 ms reaches it once in thirteen segments, and 40 ms reaches it in about half of them. hls.js seeks over the hole that leaves and plays the stream to its end, so a viewer gets an occasional jump rather than a break in the sound. Chunks around 20 ms are the case that does break: the segments are then too short for hls.js to nudge across its own `maxBufferHole`, and playback stalls where it is and does not recover.

A generator yielding one frame at a time at 25 fps is the shape that reaches the first of those. Closing it means either holding a chunk's video back until its audio is ready, which costs latency on every stream, or lowering the stall watcher's thresholds, which risks a spurious seek on every stream. Neither looks worth it for a case this narrow, and both are separable from what this PR does, so it is recorded here rather than fixed.

### The ffmpeg CI runs on

The tests here are the first in the repo to hand ffmpeg an MPEG-TS file, and the one CI ran could not read one. ffprobe exited with SIGSEGV on a file the segment muxer had just written, and ffmpeg did the same decoding a served stream. The single `.ts` test that existed before fed it the bytes `transport-stream-bytes` and patched ffprobe out, so nothing had ever reached that code path.

That build was 7.0.2, which does crash this way, and #13849 moved the pin to 8.1.2, which does not. The crash outlived the pin, because the pin was never what ran. `install-all-deps` downloads ffmpeg into `ffmpeg-bin/` and puts that directory on PATH; the directory was never ignored, so the release commit cca0297b8 swept both binaries into git on 2026-04-30, and every checkout since has laid 160 MB of 7.0.2 down at the install path. The download that would replace them only runs on a cache miss. The probe added here reported `ffprobe ... exited -11` from `ffmpeg-bin/ffprobe`, sha256 `4f231a1960d83e40`, which is one of the two blobs this PR deletes.

So the removal rides here rather than in its own PR: these are the only tests in the repo that read an MPEG-TS file, so this is the only place it can be shown to work. Unlike the pin it can be, since workflows take that action from `@main` but the checkout is the PR's own tree. With the stale cache entry dropped by hand as well, the eight tests that had been skipping ran and passed, leaving the python job with the two skips main has too, and the tests below ran against 8.1.2 on a runner for the first time. `test-hygiene.yml` still excludes `ffmpeg-bin/*` from its large-file check; that line is dead once the path is ignored, but dropping it in the same change would have pointed the check at these deletions.

The guard stays, because anyone can run the suite against an ffmpeg of their own: the tests that decode a served stream first ask whether the decoder can read an MPEG-TS file at all, and skip when it cannot. The probe names the path, hash and version banner of what it found, since CI prints no skip reasons and a skip whose cause never shows is one nobody fixes.

`js/utils/src/hls.ts` and the playlist route are shared with `gr.Audio`, so the buffer lengths, the stall watcher and `EXT-X-START` all reach streamed audio too. Starting at the first chunk is as right there as it is here, and `maxBufferLength` gates only whether hls.js fetches another fragment rather than when playback begins, so nothing starts later than it did. Worth knowing when reading a title that says video.

Closes: #13844

## Before / after Spaces

The same app on both, yielding chunks whose audio never stops, so anything heard at a boundary was added by the stream. It sweeps upward by default rather than holding a note, because the two failures sound different: silence padded in is a stutter either way, but audio dropped leaves no silence at all and only a sweep makes it audible, as a step in pitch.

Fetched from both and measured, 12 s in chunks of 0.25 s. Before: 13.375 s served for 12 s supplied, a gap at 91 boundaries, 9.46% of it silent, and the sweep up to 3995 Hz away from where its own clock puts it. After: 12.028 s, no gap at any boundary, 0.19% silent, and the sweep within the 40 Hz the measurement itself can resolve.

Listen to the finished video as well as the live stream. These are served over the network, and 12 s of 0.25 s chunks is about 48 separate fragment fetches, so the buffer runs dry and the player skips ahead. That happens on both Spaces and it is delivery, not the bytes. The replay is what separates them: on the before Space the breaks are still there when the finished video is played again, and on the after Space they are gone. The numbers above say the same thing without anyone's ears, having been measured on segments fetched from the Spaces over that same network. Running the Space's `app.py` locally against this PR's preview wheel streams through live as well.

prs.title: Import CSV and TSV files dropped on `gr.Dataframe`
prs.body:
## Description

Dropping a CSV or TSV file on a `gr.Dataframe` uploaded the file, discarded the result, and logged nothing in either the browser console or the server.

`Table.svelte` mounted `<Upload>` with no `format` prop, so it took the default `"file"`: the file went to the server and `onload` came back with a `FileData`. The reader on the other side asked for `file_data.data`, a field `FileData` does not have, fell back to an empty string, and `atob("")` threw inside the `try` that wraps `onload`. `Table.svelte` passes no `onerror`, which is why the failure surfaced nowhere. This is older than the Svelte 5 migration: `data` was last part of Upload's load payload in #5498 and #6307, the v4 rework that replaced client-side data URIs with server-side upload, and the dataframe's reader was never updated to match.

Passing `format="blob"` hands `onload` the dropped `File` itself, so the file is parsed client-side with no server round trip and no upload indicator flashing before nothing happens. `filetype` narrows the drop target to `.csv` and `.tsv`, so dropping an image no longer decodes it as table text.

A drop having been a no-op for three years, several things around it were correct only because nothing ever reached them. They land here because the repair is what makes them live:

- The drop target was never gated on `interactive`. A read-only dataframe would have started accepting dropped files and pushing new values to the backend, while already advertising `aria-readonly` on the same element. `on_file_upload` now returns early when the table is not editable, and the error channel below is withheld along with it, so a table that ignores a dropped CSV does not report on a dropped PNG either. One residual: the drag action still calls `preventDefault`, so a file dragged over a read-only table shows a copy cursor and then does nothing.
- Nothing told the user a drop was possible, which is most of why this went unnoticed. `bind:dragging` fed a variable nothing else read, and the existing `.table-wrap.dragging` highlight belongs to the cell-selection drag, `cursor: crosshair` included. The file drag now has its own class, drawn as an inset outline so nothing shifts, and the variable is renamed `file_dragging` so the two stop looking alike. `<Block>` sets `container={false}` here, which zeroes the border width, so the `border_mode={dragging ? "focus" : "base"}` pattern other components use would have been invisible.
- That highlight then turned out not to work. `create_drag` flipped `dragging` from bare `dragenter` / `dragleave` handlers, and both events bubble. This drop target wraps every cell, so crossing a cell boundary delivers `dragenter` on the cell being entered before `dragleave` on the one being left, leaving the flag false while the file is still over the table: the outline lit for the instant of each crossing and was off the rest of the time. `create_drag` now counts depth. That is in `@gradio/upload` rather than here because every drop zone with children has it, and single-child zones simply never cross an inner boundary.
- What was left of the highlight arrived as a white flash. `.table-wrap` carries a bare `transition: 150ms`, which means every property, so the outline swept in over 150ms from `currentcolor`, and `currentcolor` here is `--body-text-color`, near-white in dark mode. The declaration predates every class now on that element and the fullscreen rules are the only other thing it can still reach, so it is narrowed to the properties those change rather than removed.
- Errors still went nowhere. `<Upload>` calls `onerror` for each file `filetype` turns away, and `Table.svelte` passed no handler, so dropping a PNG would light the table up and then do nothing at all, which is the silence this PR set out to remove. `Table.svelte` takes an `onerror` prop, `Index.svelte` dispatches it as `error`, and the parse promise is caught into the same channel.
- An import could walk past constraints the rest of the component enforces. `add_row` and `add_col` refuse to change a fixed `row_count` or `col_count`, and the cell handlers refuse to write to a `static_columns` entry, but the import assigned `headers` and `values` wholesale. It now turns the file away and says why; an empty file, a file of separators alone (which parses into a header of blank names and would leave the table with unnamed columns), and a file whose rows disagree with its own header all get the same treatment, the last because a check on the header alone lets `a,b` over `1,2,3` through and pushes the ragged row to the backend. `handle_file_upload` became `parse_table_file`, returning the parsed table instead of driving two callbacks, so all of this is settled before anything is assigned.
- The drop target had nothing to say for itself. `dataframe.drop_to_upload` was handed to `<Upload>` as `aria_label`, which that component applies only on its button branch, and the dataframe sets `container_element="div"`, so the string was built and discarded. The key is translated into 33 locales and has no other consumer, and this is the change that turns it from a dead string into a live affordance, so the grid now carries `aria-describedby`. `aria-description` would have been smaller but it is ARIA 1.3: support is partial and it is missing from `svelte/elements`, so it does not type-check. Making the key live also exposed that the standalone build's fallback map carries every other key the shared components use but not this one, which would have put the raw key on screen there.
- Cell state outlived the table it pointed at. `editing` and `selected_cells` hold coordinates and nothing cleared them on import, and a stale selection reached `copy_table_data` on the next copy. `EditableCell` commits its value whenever it leaves edit mode, which cuts three ways: a narrower file left a ragged row, a shorter one threw `TypeError: Cannot set properties of undefined` out of an effect, and a file of the same shape or larger wrote the half-typed value into the table that had just replaced it, with the imported value reported as `previous_value`. The import clears that state and marks the pending edit for discard, and `handle_blur` also ignores a row the table no longer has. It checks the row alone: a value can arrive ragged from the backend, and a cell past the end of a short row still renders and still takes an edit.

The delimiter needs a word of its own. `guess_delimiter` counted raw separators, which is wrong in both directions: it found *both* candidates for a TSV carrying a comma in every row, where the order of its argument list quietly picked the comma, and it found *neither* when a separator sat inside a quoted field, so a comma-separated file named `.tsv` fell through to the extension and came out as a single column. It is gone. `parse_table_file` hands each candidate to `dsvFormat` instead, which is quote-aware for free, and takes the first that splits every line of the file into the same number of fields. Requiring all the lines to agree is what tells a real separator from one that merely sits in a header name, and a candidate that splits only the header is kept as a fallback for the case where the other does not split at all, so a file that is genuinely ragged is still reported against the shape it was meant to have. `filetype` guarantees the extension is `.csv` or `.tsv`, so trying that one first breaks a tie and settles a single-column file, where nothing splits either way. Blank lines are dropped before any of this, since one parses into a row of a single empty field and a trailing newline would otherwise be enough to refuse the whole file.

Repairing the import rather than removing it leaves both drag-and-drop statements in the tabular workflows guide accurate, so that guide is unchanged. `data_uri_to_blob` and its tests go away with the data-URI path, which had no other callers, and `HeadersWithIDs` goes with `handle_file_upload`, its last reference.

Closes: #13835

prs.title: Speed up multipage app navigation
prs.body:
This was really bugging mewhenever I'd take a look at the deployed Spaces. 

Multipage navigation currently serializes, transfers, and processes data for the entire app on every page load. This is especially costly in SSR mode because the SvelteKit server and the browser client each resolve the config and API metadata. The supplied 39-page demo sends about 2.28 MB of config plus 7.45 MB of API metadata before an individual page can render.

This PR adds an optional `page` query to `/config` and `/gradio_api/info`, forwards the current route from the SvelteKit app through `@gradio/client`, and filters components, dependencies, layout, and endpoints before copying or serializing them. Requests without `page` retain the existing full-app responses for backwards compatibility.

For `audio_debugger` in the supplied demo, the combined uncompressed config and API-info JSON is reduced from about 9.73 MB to 111 KB (roughly 87x smaller / 98.9% less data).

To see the benefits of this, try visiting the deployed Space from this PR: https://huggingface.co/spaces/gradio-pr-deploys/pr-13843-all-demos

versus one of the other deployed Spaces from any other PR, e.g. https://huggingface.co/spaces/gradio-pr-deploys/pr-13842-all-demos

prs.title: Document that None can't be used as a Dropdown choice value
prs.body:
## Description

Closes #13832 as documentation rather than a behavior change.

The original report showed that a `Dropdown` choice mapping a display label to `None` (e.g. `[("Default", None), ("Option A", "a")]`) rendered blank instead of showing "Default". An earlier version of this PR changed the frontend to prefer a choices-list match over treating `None` as "no selection."

After discussion (see [comment thread](https://github.com/gradio-app/gradio/pull/13842#issuecomment-5624285866)), we're not making that change: `None` is reserved to mean "no value selected" in `Dropdown`, and letting it double as a real choice value would remove the ability to programmatically clear the dropdown whenever `None` is also one of the choices. That's a bigger, riskier behavior change than this bug warrants.

Instead, this PR documents the limitation in the `choices` docstring and points to the existing workaround (map the choice to a placeholder value like `"default"` and convert it to `None` inside your own function). The same workaround was posted on the original issue: https://github.com/gradio-app/gradio/issues/13832#issuecomment-5781508093
