prs.title: Start all listeners of an event at once
prs.body:
## Description

Since 6.0, `DependencyManager.dispatch` runs the listeners of one event one after another, waiting for each run to finish before starting the next. In 5.x they all started at once, and nothing I could find says the new order was intended: #12170 turned `deps?.forEach(async (dep) => ...)` into an awaited `for` loop that returned after the first backend listener, and #12269 removed that `return`, which left the listeners running in sequence. This PR starts each listener as its own task again, so a quick listener no longer waits for a slow one on the same trigger.

What changes for apps, all back to how 5.x behaved:

- A listener no longer sees the outputs of the listeners registered before it on the same trigger. It gets the values from before the event. Apps that relied on registration order should chain with `.then()` or `.success()`. This includes `gr.State`: two listeners that update the same State both start from its old value, and the one that finishes last wins.
- `cancels=` takes effect right away. It is registered as a second listener on the trigger, so today `stop_btn.click(fn, cancels=[event])` only cancels after `fn` has finished.
- A validator rejection only stops its own listener. Today it returns out of the loop and the listeners registered after it never run. So a sibling that, for example, clears the textbox now runs even when the validator rejects its text; a step that should only run on accepted input belongs in a `.success()` chain.

Loading status is left as it is. When two listeners of one event write the same output, whichever finishes first marks it complete while the other is still running. That already happens on main with two buttons writing the same output, and the pending-count logic in `state.svelte.ts` that was meant to prevent it is not wired up in 6.x. Turning it back on made any run that ends without a final status leave a spinner that never stops, so it is better handled separately.

Validation errors are now cleared when a listener starts instead of when its first message arrives, so a sibling that reads the same input can no longer clear the error a validator has just shown with its first reply. Chunks sent to an open stream are skipped, since they start no new run.

This is stacked on #13991, which changes the same function, and targets its branch until that merges.

If running listeners in sequence was intended, feel free to close this.

Closes: #13992

prs.title: Run a deferred always_last event with its own event data
prs.body:
## Description

When a `trigger_mode="always_last"` event fires while its function is still running, the frontend defers it and runs it after the current call. Since the 6.0 rewrite, `DependencyManager.queue` only remembers the dependency id, so the replay re-dispatches the in-flight call's event: the deferred run gets the old `gr.EventData` (e.g. `.key_up()` ends on the first keystroke) and the old `evt.target`, and every other listener of that event runs a second time.

This stores the deferred event per dependency (the latest one wins) and replays it for that dependency only, with its own `event_data` and `target_id`. That is how it worked before 6.0 (`dep.final_event` in `Blocks.svelte`).

The replay now also happens when the running call throws, not only on completion and on a validation error. Before, an entry left in the queue by a failed call was replayed after the next run of that dependency, which only re-ran the current event. With the stored event it would replay an older one and overwrite the newer result, so the leftover has to go. Cancelling a call (e.g. a Stop button through `cancels=`) now drops its deferred event instead of running it once the cancelled call ends. A new run of the dependency also drops anything deferred before it.

Closes: #13990

prs.body:
## Description
Add native ZeroGPU support to Gradio, such that `spaces` package no longer needs to rely on monkey-patching

## Main changes
The PR introduces ZeroGPU-neutral changes:
- Support `gr.Info`, `gr.Warning` and `gr.Progress` from forked workers
  (Enable with `GRADIO_QUEUE_MULTIPROCESSING_ENABLED=true`)
- Propagate request context through queued functions and generators
- Make server startup timeout configurable via `GRADIO_START_TIMEOUT`
  (ZeroGPU tensors offloading now happens during that phase; defaults to 5 seconds)

And mounts a Gradio-tailored **`ZeroGPUMiddleware`** when running in a ZeroGPU environment

## Side changes
- Avoid creating useless ([since](https://bugs.python.org/issue42392#msg381305) [Python 3.10](https://docs.python.org/3.15/library/asyncio-sync.html#asyncio.Lock:~:text=.release()-,Changed%20in%20version%203.10%3A%20Removed%20the%20loop%20parameter,-.)) asyncio loops that raise errors during garbage collection
  (ZeroGPU startup explicitly triggers garbage collection during model packing)

prs.title: Add `gr.WebRTC`, with each stream waiting its turn in the queue
prs.body:
## Description

FastRTC's WebRTC component and the server-side machinery it needs now live in Gradio core as `gr.WebRTC`, behind an optional `webrtc` extra (`pip install "gradio[webrtc]"`, which adds aiortc). Media travels over a peer connection and never enters the queue, but each stream (from the moment the user presses Record until it ends) is one queue event. So `concurrency_limit` and `time_limit` mean what they mean for other events: a stream beyond the limit waits in line with its position and an ETA and starts by itself when a slot frees up, instead of being rejected as in FastRTC, and `time_limit` ends a stream and hands its slot to the next user.

```python
import gradio as gr
from gradio.webrtc import AdditionalOutputs

def process(frame, flip):
    out = frame[::-1] if flip else frame
    return out, AdditionalOutputs(frame.shape)

with gr.Blocks() as demo:
    webrtc = gr.WebRTC(mode="send-receive", modality="video")
    flip = gr.Checkbox(label="Flip")
    shape = gr.Textbox()
    webrtc.stream(
        process,
        inputs=[webrtc, flip],
        outputs=[webrtc, shape],
        time_limit=60,
        concurrency_limit=2,
    )
```

### Try it

Sign in first on each Space: they issue TURN credentials with the visitor's own account, as the guide recommends. All of them run this PR @ 99a70aa.

- [Component check](https://huggingface.co/spaces/hysts-debug/gradio-13907-after): video, audio and receive mode, one stream per tab for at most 30 s. Open it in a second browser tab to see the waiting position and the handoff.

Use cases on ZeroGPU, each stream holding one GPU allocation (see the note below the table):

| Space | Media | Uses | What to try |
|---|---|---|---|
| [SAM 3 tracking](https://huggingface.co/spaces/hysts-debug/gradio-13907-zerogpu-sam3-webcam) | video ⇄ video | `VideoStreamHandler`, extra input | Edit the prompt during a stream to switch what is tracked |
| [Kyutai STT](https://huggingface.co/spaces/hysts-debug/gradio-13907-zerogpu-stt) | audio → text | `mode="send"`, `AdditionalOutputs` | Speak English or French; the transcript follows live |
| [Moshi](https://huggingface.co/spaces/hysts-debug/gradio-13907-zerogpu-moshi) | audio ⇄ audio | `StreamHandler` | Interrupt it mid-sentence (use headphones) |

These apps keep the model on the GPU for the whole stream by running one `@spaces.GPU` generator per stream and feeding it through a queue, with a small bridge module in each Space. gr.WebRTC has no built-in helper for this.

### How a stream runs

1. **Record.** The frontend sets the component value to a fresh stream id and dispatches the private `stream` event (`connection="stream"`, input `[webrtc]` only, outputs `[webrtc, *extra_outputs]`, with the `concurrency_limit` and `time_limit` given to `.stream()`). No device is opened yet. While the stream waits, the component shows "Waiting · 2/3 · ~25s" next to a Cancel button; the wait counts down between the queue's estimates and is replaced by each new one. Cancelling removes the event from the line.
2. **The turn comes.** The event's first call admits the stream id (`ConnectionManager.admit` in `gradio/webrtc/connection.py`). Later calls cannot admit another id, so one place in the concurrency limit holds one stream. On `process_starts` the frontend opens the camera or microphone, fetches the RTC configuration (which the server gives only to the session whose event admitted the stream), and sends the offer through `/component_server`. An offer for an id that was not admitted is rejected, and so are an offer, an ICE candidate or an input value for an admitted id that come from another browser session than the one whose event admitted it. Stream ids are 128 random bits.
3. **Streaming.** When the handler returns `AdditionalOutputs`, the connection manager queues it and sets the event's `signal`, the same wake-up a chunk posted to `/stream/{event_id}` causes, and the next call of the event returns it as a `process_streaming` message. A watcher task wakes the event every 10 s (or every half of `time_limit`, if that is shorter) when nothing else does, because the queue ends a stream event that gets no signal for 30 s, or for its `time_limit`. Values of the other inputs reach the running stream through short private events (one when the handler asks for them, one on each input's `change`), as in FastRTC; they skip the queue, so they take no worker slot.
4. **The end.** When the peer connection closes or fails, the handler returns `CloseStream`, `time_limit` passes (counted from admission), or an admitted stream does not connect within 30 s, the server closes the peer connection at once, so the media stops on time even when every worker slot is busy. The event then delivers the outputs still pending and finishes, and the next stream in line gets the slot. The watcher keeps `time_limit` for an admitted stream, so the queue's own `time_limit` cut, which would end the event after one of those calls, does not apply to it.

### Changes to shared code

Each of these was needed for gr.WebRTC, and each also changes behavior for the existing `gr.Audio` / `gr.Image` `.stream()` events, which I think is a fix in every case. Each item comes with a test.

- **Queue: a waiting stream gives back its worker slot** (`queueing.py`). Every running event holds an entry in `Queue.active_jobs` (`max_threads`, 40 by default) from start to finish, and a streaming event spends almost all of its life in `wait_for_batch`. With 40 open `gr.Audio(streaming=True)` streams and `concurrency_limit=None`, no other event in the app could start. A streaming event now releases its entry while it waits for a chunk and takes one back (`take_worker_back`) when a chunk arrives, ahead of new events. It keeps its place in its function's `concurrency_limit`, so a GPU slot stays held for the whole stream. The dispatcher re-checks for a free entry under `delete_lock`, since two code paths now assign entries. `wait_for_batch` also pairs each event with its own wait result; it zipped the events with the unordered set that `asyncio.wait` returns, so in a batch a closed event could be taken for an awake one. A single event's wait had the same pattern: woken as its timeout ran out, it could be taken for one that timed out.
- **Queue: ETA of a waiting stream** (`broadcast_estimations`). A waiting stream got no ETA until a stream of the same function had finished once, and after that a stream without a time limit counted as freeing its slot at once (ETA close to 0). A running stream now counts as holding its slot for its `time_limit`, each stream ahead in line adds a full `time_limit`, and without a time limit there is no ETA.
- **Queue: dropped stream events end at once** (`queueing.py`). An event that its session drops (`clean_events`) is woken and removed after `wait_for_batch`, also while it waits for a worker slot, instead of holding its slot until its 30 s wait times out or running once more. Waking an event, or cancelling it while it waits, no longer leaves a wait task sleeping for the whole timeout (up to the stream's `time_limit`).
- **Queue: an acknowledged stream does not cut off the open message stream** (`acknowledge_event`, from #13585). Acknowledging the last event of a session deleted the session while the page's SSE stream was still open. A stopped stream is acknowledged before the page closes it, so the next event's messages (for example "your turn" for another stream on the same page) went to a new queue that the open SSE did not read, and arrived only after its wait timed out (forever on a Space). The session is now kept while `active_streams > 0`.
- **Queue: the resume history keeps only the latest output of a stream** (`send_message`, from #13585). For a client that may resume, every message is kept in the session's history until it is acknowledged, and a stream event sends one with each output for as long as it runs: 20 a second for a handler that returns `AdditionalOutputs` with every frame, which is about 72,000 messages after an hour, all replayed if the page reconnects. Each call of a stream event sends whole output values, so a new output now takes out of the same event's earlier messages whatever it sets again (a value, a prop such as `visible`, a token of browser-held state, a `gr.State` listed in `changed_state_ids`), and messages left with nothing are dropped. A call that skips everything (`gr.skip()`, or a wake-up with nothing new) adds nothing. The messages keep their places, so when two events write to the same component, a replay applies their writes in the order the page saw them. This holds for generator functions too, since each chunk calls them afresh (see "Route: chunk calls keep their event id" below). Logs (`gr.Info`, `gr.Warning`) and progress updates of a stream event are not kept at all: a resumed stream is only read to its end, and with its chunks keeping their event id, every chunk's logs would otherwise pile up.
- **Route: leaving the line** (`routes.py`, `/stream/{event_id}/close`). Closing a stream that had not started only marked it closed: it kept its place, added its `time_limit` to the ETA of everyone behind it, and ran once when its turn came. The route now removes it from the line and sends `process_completed`, like `/cancel`.
- **Queue: the line moves up when someone leaves it** (`remove_from_queue`, `clean_events`). With the default `status_update_rate="auto"`, estimations were sent when an event joined (to the ones behind it) and when one started, but not when a waiting event left: after a `/cancel` or a closed page, everyone behind kept their old place and ETA until the next event started. They are now sent again when an event leaves the line, for any event.
- **Route: chunk calls keep their event id** (`routes.py`, `/stream/{event_id}`). After the first chunk `LocalContext.event_id` was lost, so `gr.Info` and progress did not work in later chunks of a `gr.Audio` stream. A batched function's calls serve several events, so they get no event id, as in the first call. The event id does not make a stream continue a generator: each chunk still calls a generator function afresh with that chunk and gets whole values back (`call_process_api` neither restores nor stores `app.iterators` for `connection="stream"` functions, and their outputs are not diffs).
- **Route: server functions get the visitor's `gr.Request`** (`routes.py`, `/component_server`). The route passed the bare fastapi request. It now builds a `gr.Request` with the call's session hash and the logged-in user, as the queue does for events. gr.WebRTC's `offer` starts the handler, and handlers and `rtc_configuration` functions can take `gr.Request` / `gr.OAuthToken` (used to issue TURN credentials per visitor).
- **Helpers: `gr.Warning` / `gr.Info` without an event** (`helpers.py`, `context.py`). A stream handler runs outside any queued event, so `log_message` found no event id and printed to the server log. It now sends the message through the stream's notifier (`LocalContext.stream_notifier`) when there is one.
- **Frontend core: no resuming a stream after a reload** (`dependency.ts`). With session resume (#13585), a reloaded page resumed every running event, streams included. A stream cannot continue in a new page, so the resumed event only held its slot until it timed out (30 s for the next user in line, measured; 115 ms after the change). `resume()` now asks the server to end resumed `connection="stream"` events and reads what it sends up to the event's end, so the outputs sent while the page was reloading are shown, the `.change` listeners of the `gr.State` values the stream changed run, and the `.then()` / `.success()` chain (or `.failure()`, if it had failed) follows; a stream that was still waiting in line runs `.failure()` and `.then()`, as a cancelled event does. The end is a message from the server in every case (a stream that had ended is replayed with its completion, one still waiting in line is removed, a running one is closed), so this does not depend on how fast the connection to the server opens or how long the stream's last call waits for a worker: there is no deadline, and messages that stop without an end (which the server never does) leave the chain alone rather than counting as a success. The JS client's `close_stream()` takes `{ read_to_end: true }` for this, which keeps the iterator open until that message. The completion of a stream removed from the line carries no outputs (`output={}`, as for `/cancel`), and the client passed its missing `data` on as `undefined`, so `resume()` threw before acknowledging the event or running its chain; it now reads as no outputs.
- **Frontend core: a stream ended on the page still finishes on the server** (`dependency.ts`). When the page ended a stream (the user's Stop, a handler's `CloseStream`, or a server-side end that the page notices), it closed the event's iterator at once and acknowledged the event, so outputs still pending on the server were dropped (a receive-mode generator's `yield AdditionalOutputs(result); yield CloseStream()` never showed `result`, and under load the last outputs of any stream were lost) and only `.then()` ran, never `.success()`. This is how every streaming component behaves on `7.0-dev`, `gr.Audio` and `gr.Image` included. The page now asks the server to end the stream and reads the event to its end, as `resume()` does: the last outputs are shown and `.success()` (or `.failure()`) runs. A stream stopped before its turn came never ran, so it runs `.failure()` and `.then()` instead, as a stream stopped through `cancels=` does. It leaves the component's status alone meanwhile, since the page has settled it already and a new stream of the same event may have started. For gr.WebRTC, `/stream/{event_id}/close` ends a running stream through its connection manager instead of closing the event, so the event delivers every pending output before it finishes and fails if the handler has just failed. For `gr.Audio` and `gr.Image`, a closed stream is not called again (#13983), so the page gets the output of its last chunk. The completion does not report that chunk's `gr.State` changes again, which would run their `.change` listeners a second time.
- **Frontend core: `close_stream` closes only stream events, and only stream events close a stream** (`dependency.ts`). `close_stream(id)` closed every running event the component triggers, so a `change` handler of the same component was cut off. And the completion of any event marked its input components' `stream_state` as "closed", so a short event that takes the streaming component as input ended its stream in the UI.
- **Frontend core: toast events from components** (`Blocks.svelte`, `toast.ts`). A component could already dispatch `error` / `warning` / `info` with a message. These now also take a toast object (message, title, duration, visibility and type), so gr.WebRTC can show what a handler raises. A `gr.Success` toast is dispatched as `info` with `type: "success"`: a `success` dispatch still runs the component's `success` listeners, since a custom component may declare such an event.
- **JS client: an acknowledged event is no longer open** (`utils/submit.ts`, from #13585). A stream stopped on the page is acknowledged before the server completes it, so the server dropped its `process_completed` and the client kept the event in `unclosed_events` for the life of the page. Every normal close of the SSE stream then made the client reopen it, and a reopen that lost the race against the next acknowledgement (which deletes the finished session) failed with `HTTPException(404)` inside `sse_stream` ("response already started" in the logs). Stopping a `gr.Audio` stream does the same on `7.0-dev`. This is not the cancelled-stream cause of #13895 that #13925 addresses for sse_v4. Messages that still arrive for an acknowledged event (its completion, an output already on the way) are now dropped instead of being kept in `pending_stream_messages` for the life of the page, and the event's iterator ends when it is acknowledged (dropping its generator diff state too), so a cancelled event no longer waits for a completion that is dropped. Since acknowledging now closes a run, the page acknowledges the run that failed (`dependency.ts`) rather than the latest run of the same event, which with `trigger_mode="multiple"` could be another one still going. `DependencyManager.cancel()` runs the `.failure()` / `.then()` chain of a run it cancels, so the loop that read that run, which now ends when the run is acknowledged, leaves the chain to it; `.then()` ran twice otherwise.
- **ZeroGPU headers on the server function calls that start GPU work** (`client.ts`, `helpers/zerogpu.ts`, `components/base.py`, `js/core/src/init.svelte.ts`). The client sent the visitor's ZeroGPU headers (`x-zerogpu-token` / `x-zerogpu-uuid`, provided by the embedding Hugging Face page) only with `queue/join`. gr.WebRTC's `offer` is a server function call that starts the handler, so GPU work in it was charged to an anonymous visitor. A server function can now ask for the headers with `@server(zerogpu_headers=True)`: the component's config lists it in `zerogpu_server_fns`, and the frontend passes `{zerogpu_headers: true}` to `Client.component_server` for it. Only `offer` does, and other server functions (gr.FileExplorer, gr.ImageEditor and so on) do not wait for the embedding page. Calls made at once (a connection's ICE candidates) share one request, and a call waits at most 5 s for an answer before it goes out without them. Queue submissions keep their own request as before, and outside a ZeroGPU iframe nothing changes.

### What is in the port

- `gradio/webrtc/`: `handlers.py` (`StreamHandler`, `AsyncStreamHandler`, `AudioVideoStreamHandler`, `AsyncAudioVideoStreamHandler`, `VideoStreamHandler`, `AsyncVideoStreamHandler`, `VideoOptions`), `tracks.py` (the aiortc tracks that feed frames to a handler and back), `connection.py` (admission, offer/answer with trickle ICE, one peer connection and one handler instance per stream, data channel messages), `bitrate.py` (`video_bitrate`), and `utils.py` (`AdditionalOutputs`, `CloseStream`, audio helpers and the audio frame encoder). Everything except `tracks.py`, `connection.py` and `bitrate.py` imports without aiortc, so `from gradio.webrtc import ...` works on a plain install and the component can be constructed; `.stream()` raises an `ImportError` pointing at the extra.
- `gradio/components/webrtc.py`: the component, with `mode` (`send-receive`, `send`, `receive`), `modality` (`video`, `audio`, `audio-video`), `rtc_configuration` (dict, or a sync/async function or callable object resolved per connection so short-lived TURN credentials work), `server_rtc_configuration`, `webcam_options`, `microphone_options`, `rtp_params`, `video_bitrate`, `allow_extra_tracks` and `stream_options` (`gr.StreamOptions`).
- `js/webrtc`: a Svelte 5 package with the webcam, microphone and receive-only players, FastRTC's pulsing-icon and waveform visualizers, and the signalling helpers.
- A rewrite of the WebRTC guide (`07_streaming/02_object-detection-from-webcam-with-webrtc.md`), including how to deploy on Spaces, a docs page, and a `demo/webrtc_video_flip` demo.

### What changes compared to FastRTC's component

<details>
<summary>API, behavior and bugs fixed on the way (click to expand)</summary>

- **A stream waits for its turn.** FastRTC rejected a connection with "concurrency limit reached" once `len(pcs) >= concurrency_limit`, and `time_limit` was a timer on the connection. Both are now the queue's (see above). `concurrency_limit="default"` follows `Blocks.queue(default_concurrency_limit=...)`.
- **`outputs` carries the additional outputs.** `AdditionalOutputs(a, b)` updates the non-WebRTC components listed in `outputs`, in order, like the return values of any other event. `on_additional_outputs()` is gone, and so is FastRTC's long-lived output event, which ran with the default concurrency limit of 1, so a second user's outputs waited until the first user disconnected. Outputs are delivered oldest first; if more than 64 are waiting, the oldest are dropped.
- **Handlers receive exactly the extra inputs.** Video functions get `fn(frame, *extra)`, receive-mode generators get `fn(*extra)`, and `StreamHandler.latest_args` holds the extra values. FastRTC prepended a `"__webrtc_value__"` placeholder in some paths and not in others, and after gradio-app/fastrtc#321 and #414 a video handler used through the Gradio component drops its first extra input. `wait_for_args()` asks the page for the values only until they have arrived, then returns at once, since every change of an input updates `latest_args`; FastRTC's docs call it in `emit()`, and it sent a request to the page on every call.
- **A handler class can be passed.** `webrtc.stream(EchoHandler, ...)` creates one instance per connection; an instance still works through `copy()`, and passing an instance without `copy()` is rejected at wiring time. An `async def` function or async generator is rejected there too, instead of failing on the first frame as in FastRTC; async code goes in an `AsyncVideoStreamHandler`. So is an async handler class whose `start_up` is a plain `def`, which FastRTC ran on the event loop before raising.
- **Video-only streams can use a handler class.** In FastRTC, `start_up()` and `shutdown()` exist only on audio and audio-video handler classes, and a video stream takes a function per frame. A stream that holds something for its whole duration, such as one ZeroGPU allocation or a tracker's state on the GPU, therefore had to be an audio-video stream, and the page opened a microphone it never used. `VideoStreamHandler` / `AsyncVideoStreamHandler` give `modality="video"` the same `video_receive()` / `video_emit()` methods with `start_up()` and `shutdown()`, in `mode="send-receive"`. FastRTC's `VideoStreamHandler(fn, fps, skip_frames)`, which wraps a frame function with its frame settings, is renamed `VideoOptions` so that the class can take the name next to `StreamHandler` and `AudioVideoStreamHandler`. With `modality="audio"`, `.stream()` now accepts only audio handler classes, so a video-only class is rejected instead of being run as audio.
- **Connection state is not kept on the component instance.** A `gr.update()` on the component gives the session a new instance, and `/component_server` then calls `offer` on that instance. Each `.stream()` call therefore gets a connection manager that its queue event holds, and signalling and input updates find it by the stream's id. The component id is not enough for that, since `@gr.render` gives a keyed component the same id in every session and every render. The component stays picklable as a side effect. In a `@gr.render`, the component has to be created in the same render as its `.stream()` call, which raises otherwise: the page learns that a component has a stream handler from its config, and a render sends only the config of the components it creates.
- **Sync video handlers run in a worker thread.** FastRTC calls a plain video function, a receive-mode video generator, and the sync `video_receive()` / `video_emit()` of audio-video handlers directly on the event loop that also serves the app, so a slow handler stalls every other connection and every HTTP route. With a handler that blocks for 300 ms per frame, a request to `/gradio_api/queue/status` took about 400 ms instead of 3 ms, and two connections with a 66 ms handler shared one connection's frame rate (14 fps in total). These calls now go through `anyio.to_thread.run_sync`, as the sync audio handlers already did. With the same handlers, HTTP stays at 2 to 3 ms and two connections get 14 fps each. So do the sync `emit()` of audio handlers and receive-mode audio generators, which FastRTC ran in the default executor without the visitor's context, so that a `@spaces.GPU` call made there did not carry the visitor's ZeroGPU headers. The handler threads have their own limiter, so busy streams do not take the `max_threads` tokens that Gradio's sync event listeners share.
- **`skip_frames` defaults to `True`.** Incoming frames are buffered without a bound, and with FastRTC's default every frame is processed in order, so a handler slower than the camera falls further behind for as long as the stream runs (about 8 s behind after 28 s with a 66 ms handler on a 20 fps camera, with memory growing alongside). The default now processes the newest frame and drops the ones that arrived in the meantime. `VideoOptions(fn, skip_frames=False)` restores the old behavior. `VideoOptions(fn, fps=...)` now also limits how often the function runs in the send modes (FastRTC used `fps` only in receive mode and when no frame had arrived), so `fps=5` cuts the load of a heavy model on a 30 fps camera. The default of 30 matches the default camera constraint; with a faster camera, pass a higher `fps` to process every frame. This is the lag reported in gradio-app/fastrtc#152. The `video_receive()` of a handler class gets the same treatment: when it is slower than the camera, it gets the newest frame instead of every one in turn, where FastRTC queued them without a bound. Frames that will be skipped are dropped as they arrive, so a handler that is busy for a while holds one waiting frame rather than all of them.
- **Video frames are RGB, like the numpy values of `gr.Image` and `gr.Video`.** FastRTC hands handlers BGR arrays and expects BGR back, so code moved from a `gr.Image` streaming app swapped red and blue. OpenCV-based code converts with `cv2.cvtColor`, as the guide's YOLO example now does. A frame returned as `float32` (e.g. a model's output in [0, 1]) or `uint16` is scaled to `uint8`, and an RGBA or grayscale frame converted to RGB, the way `gr.Image` does, where FastRTC's encoder rejected it and ended the stream.
- **Audio frames have `gr.Audio`'s numpy layout.** FastRTC hands `receive()` the resampler's packed array, `(1, samples)` for mono and an interleaved `(1, 2 * samples)` for stereo, and takes channels-first arrays from `emit()` with an explicit `"mono"` / `"stereo"` third element. Audio now goes both ways as `(sample_rate, array)` shaped `(samples,)` or `(samples, 2)`, like `gr.Audio(type="numpy")`. Integer arrays are scaled as `gr.Audio` does. Float arrays of any precision are taken as values in [-1, 1] and, unlike `gr.Audio`, are not scaled to each array's own peak, which in a stream would play every chunk, quiet ones included, at full volume. Channels-first arrays and the three-element form fail with a message that explains the layout. Float values past full scale are clipped when converted to int16, instead of wrapping around to the opposite sign.
- **Errors and messages in a handler work as in other events.** FastRTC turned every exception into a `WebRTCError` and sent `str(e)` to the page: a `gr.Error` was shown wrapped in quotes, any other exception showed its internal message regardless of `show_error`, an error in an audio-video handler's `video_receive` was never shown and left the stream running, and `gr.Warning` / `gr.Info` went to the server log only. Errors now use the same payload as events and end the stream, and `gr.Warning` / `gr.Info` / `gr.Success` are shown on that stream's page. The stream's queue event then fails too, also when the handler cannot be created (its last call raises the error, hidden when the page has shown it already, over the data channel or from the offer's answer, and shown otherwise, for example when the handler fails before the data channel opens), so `.failure()` runs instead of `.success()`, as for a `gr.Audio` stream whose function raises, and a page that resumes the event sees the failure. `WebRTCError` is gone; raise `gr.Error`. An `rtc_configuration` function that fails, or returns something other than a dict, is shown by the same rule, and a configuration request that fails on the page is reported instead of connecting without the ICE servers.
- **A handler that ends its stream does not log an aiortc error.** When a handler returns `CloseStream` (or a receive-mode generator runs out), FastRTC's tracks return `None` from `recv()`, which aiortc's sender hands to its encoder, so every stream that the handler ended logged a traceback. The tracks now raise `MediaStreamError`, aiortc's signal that a track is over, and so does a handler that fails (after its error has been reported), instead of a second traceback from aiortc. Also, an audio handler's `emit()` or a receive-mode audio generator is no longer called again after it returns `CloseStream`; FastRTC kept calling it until the track had played what came before.
- **Audio plays to its end, and receive mode does not run far ahead.** When a generator ran out or a handler returned `CloseStream`, the resampler's last few milliseconds were dropped, so a clip of 20 ms or less played nothing at all. They are now flushed and padded to a whole frame. A receive-mode generator also waits once it is about a second ahead of playback, where FastRTC buffered without a bound (a generator faster than real time kept growing memory, and the `AdditionalOutputs` it yielded ran ahead of the audio). Handler audio stays unbounded, since `clear_queue()` drops what `emit()` returned so far and a bound would leave more of it in the handler. After a pause of a receive-mode generator (a model call between two sentences), the audio that follows plays in real time, where FastRTC sent it at once to catch up with its clock.
- **Handlers can take `gr.Request`, `gr.OAuthProfile` and `gr.OAuthToken`**, like an event listener: a stream function (and the `start_up` method of a handler class) gets the values of the visitor who started the stream. So can an `rtc_configuration` function.
- **The handler sees the webcam the way the preview shows it, as in `gr.Image`.** FastRTC mirrors only the local preview, so with a front camera the picture flips left to right when a stream starts. The client now says in its offer whether its preview is mirrored, and the server mirrors the frames before the handler gets them (front cameras by default since #13926). `webcam_options=gr.WebcamOptions(mirror=False)` gives the handler the camera's own view.
- **`video_bitrate` sets the bitrate range of the video.** aiortc starts its VP8 encoder at 500 kbps and caps it at 1.5 Mbps with module constants, and Chrome scales down the picture it sends while its estimate is low: on a Space with a laptop webcam (1280x720 requested), Chrome sent 640x360 for about 25 s of a 28 s stream. `video_bitrate={"min": 1000, "start": 1500, "max": 4000}` (kbps) is applied as the `x-google-*-bitrate` parameters in the answer for the video the browser sends, and through a per-connection encoder for the video the server sends back. With it, Chrome moved to 960x540 within 1.5 to 3 s and reached 1280x720. The default (`None`) leaves both sides as they are.
- **The look of the stream controls is set with `stream_options=gr.StreamOptions(...)`.** FastRTC's flat `icon`, `icon_button_color`, `pulse_color`, `icon_radius` and `button_labels` parameters are grouped into one options class, like `gr.Audio`'s `waveform_options`. `button_labels` stays because it is the only way to word one component's buttons differently (`gr.I18n` cannot override built-in keys), and its values can be `gr.I18n` translations. The icon is sent as served file data, like `gr.Button`'s, so it also loads when the app is mounted under a path.
- **Media constraints use Gradio's option classes.** `track_constraints` and `mirror_webcam` become `webcam_options=gr.WebcamOptions(...)` and `microphone_options=gr.MicrophoneOptions(...)` (from #13931). The given constraints are merged over the defaults instead of replacing them, so `gr.MicrophoneOptions(constraints={"echoCancellation": False})` keeps the mono 24 kHz input that voice handlers expect.
- **The microphone is held only while recording.** FastRTC's audio UI reopens the microphone right after a recording stops (since gradio-app/fastrtc#15), so the browser shows it as in use for as long as the component is on screen. It is now opened when a recording starts and released when it stops, fails or the component unmounts, like `gr.Audio` after #13901. With `modality="audio-video"`, the webcam preview likewise keeps only the camera: access asks for both in one prompt, then lets the microphone go until a stream starts. Before, the preview held the microphone between streams, and another app on the computer could get silence from it.
- **A brief disconnection does not end the stream.** FastRTC's players ended the stream as soon as the connection reported `disconnected`, a state that often recovers by itself (a phone switching from Wi-Fi to cellular, a short Wi-Fi drop), so the user had to wait in line again. The stream now ends only if the connection stays disconnected for 5 s.
- **A double click on stop does not start a new stream.** Stop and start are the same button, so the second click of a double click started a new stream, which joined the queue and could take a GPU turn. The button now ignores clicks for 500 ms after a stop.
- **The webcam can be turned off.** Once accessed, the camera stayed on for as long as the page was open. A button in the top right of the idle preview releases it, like `gr.Image`'s remove button.
- **An audio-video stream keeps the chosen camera.** FastRTC takes the device of the stream's first track as the camera in use, but a camera and microphone stream lists the microphone first, so after switching to another camera (for example a phone's back camera) the preview went back to the first one when a stream ended.
- **Leaving the page ends the stream at once.** On a closed tab the stream ended only when the queue gave up waiting for the page to reconnect (5 s later), and a handler that holds a GPU kept it that long. The components now close their connection on `pagehide`, and a page restored from the back/forward cache shows the stream as ended. A device that disappears without closing anything (crash, lost network) is still only noticed by ICE consent checks, after about 30 s.
- **A sync `shutdown()` runs in a worker thread**, like the handler's other sync methods. FastRTC calls it on the event loop, so a `shutdown()` that joins a worker or waits for a queue to drain stalled every connection and HTTP route while it ran. The queue gives an ended stream's place to the next user before its handler has shut down, so with `concurrency_limit=1` the next handler is created only once that is done (waiting up to 5 s, once per shutdown, so one that never finishes delays only the next stream). An error in `shutdown()` is logged and does not fail a stream that ended normally., and a model that each handler loads is never in memory twice. With a higher limit the next stream does not wait.
- **A receive-mode generator is closed when its stream ends.** FastRTC left it suspended at its last `yield`, so a `finally` block or `with` statement in it ran only whenever Python collected it. It is now closed once a call still running in its worker thread returns, and with `concurrency_limit=1` the next stream waits for that as it does for `shutdown()`.
- **A handler may have nothing to send yet.** Returning `None`, or `AdditionalOutputs` alone (which its type allows), from `video_emit()` failed the stream in FastRTC, and so did yielding them from a receive-mode video generator; a receive-mode audio generator that yielded them ended its stream. The track now asks again a frame later and the page keeps showing the last frame, for example while `start_up()` loads a model. A frame function that returns only `AdditionalOutputs` in `mode="send-receive"` sends the frame back unchanged. An audio `emit()` with nothing ready is asked again after 5 ms rather than at once, which kept a CPU core busy per stream.
- **A slow audio handler call is waited for, not started again.** FastRTC's audio loop gave up on a call after 60 s and started the next one while the first kept running in its worker thread: two `emit()` calls at once on the handler's state, or `generator already executing` for a receive-mode generator whose next chunk took over a minute (a ZeroGPU wait, for example). The call is now awaited until it returns or the stream stops, with a warning in the log every 60 s. Each call also runs as its own task, so on Python 3.12+ an async `emit()` that returns without awaiting no longer holds the event loop.
- **`receive()` gets one chunk per incoming frame.** The input resampler made chunks as long as the incoming frame counted in samples at the handler's rate, so with `input_sample_rate=16000` `receive()` got 60 ms every third frame.
- **A stream can be stopped from another event.** FastRTC's `update_connection(webrtc_id, "closed")` asked the page over the data channel to close the stream, for any id. `stream()` now returns its event, so `stop.click(None, cancels=[stream_event])` ends the stream like any other running event, and only the page that started it can.
- **`interactive=False` disables the controls.** FastRTC's frontend never read `interactive`, so Record still started a stream. In "send" and "send-receive", Record and the device access button are now disabled while the component is not interactive; a running or waiting stream can still be stopped.
- **The page side of connecting.** The "Taking a while to connect" warning now fires when the connection has not connected 10 s after it was created; it was cancelled once the answer arrived, so it never showed in the usual VPN or strict NAT case. Audio sent back on an audio-video stream is unmuted whatever order its tracks arrive in, and Firefox's empty end-of-candidates is not sent to the server.
- **A handler that cannot start shows its error.** If creating the stream's handler raised (its constructor, or `copy()` for an instance) or the offer could not be applied, FastRTC left the peer connection registered and the page showed a generic connection error. The stream now ends at once and the page shows the error by the same rule as an event's.
- **A send-mode stream leaves nothing running.** In `mode="send"` the server reads the track itself, and that reader waited for the next frame forever after the stream ended. It now ends with the stream.
- **TURN credentials go only to a stream that has its turn.** FastRTC's `turn` server function answered any caller at any time, so with the author's own TURN account a script could keep fetching credentials billed to them. `get_rtc_configuration` now answers only the browser session whose stream this component's queue event admitted, and only until that stream ends (a turn for one gr.WebRTC does not unlock another's configuration), and resolves an `rtc_configuration` function once per stream however often the page asks, so `concurrency_limit` and `time_limit` bound the TURN traffic too, as the guide says. For the same reason, ICE candidates that arrive before the offer are kept only for a stream admitted for the sending session.
- **A webcam that cannot be opened says so.** Errors other than a denied permission (no camera, a camera that another app holds, constraints the device cannot meet) were thrown without a message to the user.
- **No librosa, no pydub helpers.** The only use of librosa was resampling when a handler changed its output sample rate mid-stream; the encoder now recreates its `av.AudioResampler` instead. The mp3 helpers are not ported.
- **Spaces and Colab without `rtc_configuration` raise** at `.stream()` time, with a pointer to the guide. On Spaces the guide recommends issuing Cloudflare TURN credentials with each visitor's own `gr.OAuthToken`, so that visitors do not use up the author's monthly quota (tested on a Space: the browser relays through TURN, and the server needs no TURN of its own).
- **Not ported:** `variant="textbox"`, `full_screen`, `send_input_on`, the `phone_mode` and deprecated `output_frame_size` handler options, the websocket and telephone transports, the TURN credential helpers, `ReplyOnPause` and the STT/TTS models.

</details>

### Measurements

<details>
<summary>Start latency, output lag and worker slots (click to expand)</summary>

Headless Chromium on one machine, fake camera at 20 fps, a handler that returns each frame with `AdditionalOutputs(server time)`, `concurrency_limit=None`. Output lag is the browser's clock minus the server time in the output.

| | 1 stream, max_threads=40 | 5 streams, max_threads=2 | 5 streams, max_threads=40 |
|---|---|---|---|
| Click to queue join / offer sent / connected | 37 / 60 / 115 ms | ~49 / ~117 / ~240 ms | similar |
| Output lag p50 / p95 | 6 / 7 ms | 20 / 26 ms | 20 / 28 ms |
| Output updates per second per user | 20.6 | 20.8 | 21.0 |
| Plain button p50 / max (includes Playwright overhead) | 64 / 67 ms | 65 / 81 ms | 76 / 133 ms |
| Busy worker slots, max | 1 | 2 | 4 |

The `max_threads=2` column is the one the worker slot change is about: before it, two open streams exhausted both slots and the button never returned. The lag goes from 6 to 20 ms with five streams whether there are 2 or 40 slots, so it comes from five browsers encoding and decoding video on one machine, not from waiting for a slot. With `concurrency_limit=1` and two users, the second one starts 109 to 130 ms after the first stops or reloads. I did not measure FastRTC's direct connection for comparison; the queue adds the join and the turn before the offer, 60 ms here with nobody waiting.

</details>

### Known issues

- The per-stream watcher (polling every 0.25 s, waking the event every 10 s) exists mostly to work around the queue's fixed 30 s chunk timeout and its `time_limit` cut, and to notice that the queue dropped the event. A queue-level hook (a per-function "no chunk timeout" option and a callback when an event finishes or is cleaned) would let the component drop the polling.
- Resuming streams take worker slots before new events. While streams keep waiting for a slot, for example when running streams outnumber worker slots (`concurrency_limit=None` and more than `max_threads` streams) or when long jobs hold the other slots and a few busy streams take turns on the last one, steady chunk traffic can hold off every other queued event indefinitely, new streams included (gr.WebRTC's input updates skip the queue). Before this change streams held their slots all the time, so those events could not start at all in either case and it is not a regression, but a fair policy would be better. Waiting for a slot also polls every 1 ms, as the dispatcher does, but once per waiting stream, so the wakeups grow with the number of streams waiting (40 waiting streams wake the event loop about 40,000 times a second); an `asyncio.Event` set when a slot frees would remove the polling.
- An ended stream gives its concurrency slot to the next user only after its event's last call, which needs a worker slot. The media stops on time, but with every worker busy the next user waits for one.
- A turn can come much earlier than the countdown says (someone ahead cancels, or the running stream stops early), and the stream then starts at once, opening the camera or microphone, even if the user stepped away from the page.
- A stream that ends on the server side is closed by the page afterwards too, and that `POST /stream/{id}/close` gets a 404 (console error only).
- On Spaces, the server log occasionally shows an `HTTPException` 404 from `sse_stream`, followed by "Caught handled exception, but response already started": a page's message stream asked for a session the queue had already deleted. Nothing breaks on the page. It did not reproduce locally or on the after Space with session tracing, so I could not tell whether it comes from this PR or is already on `7.0-dev` (restarting the server while a page has an event running causes it on `7.0-dev` too).
- If ICE stalls after the answer (no TURN behind a strict NAT), the page warns after 10 s that connecting takes a while, and the stream ends after 30 s without saying why.
- ZeroGPU: a function handler that calls a `@spaces.GPU` function pays the GPU acquisition on every frame. Holding one allocation per stream works with app code today (the use-case Spaces under [Try it](#try-it) do it). A streaming API on the ZeroGPU side is being discussed internally ([Slack](https://huggingface.slack.com/archives/C05GV830X3K/p1792393308685939)), so this PR adds nothing for it to Gradio.
- Peer connections are process-local, so multi-replica Spaces need sticky routing, as queue events do today.
- When a handler ends an audio stream with `CloseStream`, the last ~100 ms the browser has received but not yet played can be cut off: the page stops its receivers on `end_stream`, and the server closes the connection right after the last frame. Inherited from FastRTC; a fix needs a short grace on both sides.
- Between two calls of a stream event, the event has no worker slot, and the queue sends `gr.Info` / `gr.Warning` / progress only for events in a slot. A message from a background thread the handler started, or a progress update in a call shorter than the progress interval (0.1 s), is dropped or delayed. Before this change a stream held its slot throughout, but its calls after the first had no event id, so their messages never reached the page at all.

### Left for follow-ups

These are proposed in #13907 or its parent #13619 but not covered here. Whether to do them is still open.

- **Adapting to the deployment (item 3 of #13907).** The idea is that on a busy Space a stream keeps to `time_limit` and hands its slot to the next user, while a stream with nobody waiting behind it, as in a local app, can keep going. In this PR `time_limit` is a hard upper bound in every case. I would keep it as the app author's upper bound, since on ZeroGPU visitors need to know how much quota one stream can use, and make running past it opt-in, for example with a minimum and a maximum that the author sets.
- **WebRTC without the component (`gr.Server`, #13619).** Streams work only through `gr.WebRTC` for now: signalling goes through the component's server functions, and a stream is admitted by the component's private stream event. `gr.Server` has neither. A server-side entry point such as `server.webrtc(handler, ...)` (like FastRTC's `Stream.mount(app)`) and a `@gradio/client` helper that joins the queue, waits for the turn and negotiates would make it usable from a custom frontend. The handler classes, the tracks and most of the connection manager would carry over as they are.

Part of: #13907

## Before / after Spaces

There is no before Space, since `gr.WebRTC` does not exist on `7.0-dev` without this PR. The after Spaces are under [Try it](#try-it) at the top.

## Testing

The backend tests (`test/components/test_webrtc.py`) join the queue and negotiate real aiortc peer connections against a running app. The frontend tests mount the component with a fake `RTCPeerConnection` and real `MediaStream`s. No Playwright spec is added, since CI has no media devices and the functional suite is the most expensive layer. Instead I drove the three modes end to end in headless Chromium with its fake camera and microphone (two users in line, reloads while streaming and while waiting, leaving the page), and checked on private Spaces on laptops and phones, including TURN with visitor OAuth credentials, and on a ZeroGPU Space whose app holds one GPU allocation per stream with its own bridge code (this PR only makes the server function calls carry the visitor's ZeroGPU headers).

## AI Disclosure

We encourage the use of AI tooling in creating PRs, but the any non-trivial use of AI needs be disclosed. E.g. if you used Claude to write a first draft, you should mention that. Trivial tab-completion doesn't need to be disclosed. You should self-review all PRs, especially if they were generated with AI.

## 🎯 PRs Should Target Issues

Before your create a PR, please check to see if there is [an existing issue](https://github.com/gradio-app/gradio/issues) for this change. If not, please create an issue before you create this PR, unless the fix is very small. 

Not adhering to this guideline will result in the PR being closed. 

## Testing and Formatting Your Code

1. PRs will only be merged if tests pass on CI. We recommend at least running the backend tests locally, please set up [your Gradio environment locally](https://github.com/gradio-app/gradio/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md) and run the backed tests: `bash scripts/run_backend_tests.sh`

2. Please run these bash scripts to automatically format your code: `bash scripts/format_backend.sh`, and (if you made any changes to non-Python files) `bash scripts/format_frontend.sh`

prs.title: Stream each queued event on its own request (sse_v4)
prs.body:
## Description

A queued event currently takes two requests that have to reach the same server process. `POST /queue/join` enqueues the event and returns an event id. A separate, session-wide `GET /queue/data` stream then delivers the event's messages. Behind a load balancer without session affinity, or with several workers in one container (`gunicorn`/`uvicorn --workers N`), the two requests regularly reach different processes. The event then fails with `session_not_found` (which reloads the page), or it hangs if the second process has an older message queue for that session.

This PR adds `sse_v4`: **one request per event**. `/queue/join` answers a request that sends `Accept: text/event-stream` with that event's own messages (estimation, progress, logs, generations with diffs, completion) and ends the stream when the event completes. Nothing about the event depends on a second request reaching the same process.

- **Cancelling is closing the request.** The connection always leads back to the process running the event, so cancel needs no routing. On disconnect, the server does what `/cancel` does, but for that one event: it removes the event from the queue or cancels its task, and closes its iterator. A batched run is never cancelled, since it also carries other sessions' events; the dropped event is simply marked dead. `/cancel` still works for these events and ends their stream with the usual completion message.
- **Existing clients are unaffected.** The config keeps `"protocol": "sse_v3"` and adds `"supported_protocols": ["sse_v3", "sse_v4"]`. Older JS and Python clients only read `protocol`; advertising `sse_v4` there would have broken them. Their requests take the unchanged legacy path, because they don't send `Accept: text/event-stream`.
- **Validation errors and a full queue keep their HTTP status (422/503).** These are returned before any streaming starts.
- **Clients.**
  - `@gradio/client` uses `sse_v4` whenever the server lists it. The per-event message handling is shared with `sse_v3`: it was moved out of the v3 branch, not rewritten.
  - The Python client reads each event's stream on its own thread, into the same per-event queue the shared `sse_v3` reader fills. `Job.cancel()` closes that request as well as posting `/cancel`.

This removes the join/stream split, which is the most common way multi-replica deployments fail today. It does not make Gradio fully stateless across replicas. `gr.State`, component updates, `@gr.render`, uploaded and output files (unless on shared storage), and `auth=` logins still live in one process. Apps using them still need session affinity; that's follow-up work.

It also removes the bug class behind #13895: for sse_v4 events there is no session-wide message queue that one dropped stream can delete. The legacy sse_v3 path, which older clients still use, is unchanged and still has that bug; a small separate fix on `main` would cover it.

Closes: #13895

Related: #10487, #9136. Overlaps with #13585 (Resume sessions), which builds resume on the shared `queue/data` stream. The two touch the same files, and their designs will need reconciling: resuming from an in-memory buffer is inherently tied to one process.

### Behavior changes worth reviewing

1. **Stop takes effect immediately.** Output that was generated but not yet delivered when Stop is clicked is dropped. With sse_v3 it still arrived while `/cancel` and `/reset` were in flight. `test stopping generation` clicked Stop before the first chunk and relied on that; it now waits for the first chunk, which also removes the race under sse_v3.
2. **Closing an event's request cancels it**, including a running async function, the same way `/cancel` does. Before, a dropped `queue/data` stream only marked the session's events dead, so a running non-generator function ran to completion and its result was thrown away.
3. **One connection per in-flight event, instead of one per tab while events are pending.** An app that runs one event at a time uses the same number of connections as before. Several concurrent events from one tab now use several connections, so on plain HTTP/1.1 the browser's six-connections-per-origin limit applies to them. Hitting the limit delays events rather than failing them, since there's no second request left to starve. HTTP/2, which most TLS proxies speak to browsers, removes the limit. There's no client-side cap in this PR; that's an open question.

To keep what the frontend sees on cancel identical to sse_v3, the client reports the same completion `/cancel` would have injected (`output: {}`), and resolves `cancel()` only after listeners have handled it. The frontend marks the event complete only after `cancel()` resolves; without this ordering, a Stop left an Error badge on the output.

### Not in this PR

- The `/call/{api_name}` REST API is still two requests.
- Making session state, files and auth work across replicas.

## Before and after, across two replicas

Two processes of one stateless app, behind a round-robin proxy with no affinity, used from a real browser:

- **sse_v3** (the same app, with `supported_protocols` stripped from the config): an event whose join reached replica A and whose `queue/data` stream reached replica B spun forever. B still had this session's message queue from an earlier event, so there wasn't even a `session_not_found`.
- **sse_v4**: every event completed, whichever replica got it. Each was a single `POST /queue/join`. Stop cancelled a running async job on the replica that ran it: its per-tick log stopped at the moment of the click, and no `/cancel` request was made.

## Testing

Run locally on macOS with Python 3.10 (the CI version), without torch/transformers installed:

- **Backend**, `test/test_queueing.py` + `test/test_routes.py`: 219 passed, including 6 new tests in `TestOwnEventStream`. They cover the config, one-request streaming, a 422 before streaming, a dropped stream cancelling only its own event, `/cancel` ending the stream, and a client leaving before the response starts. One run had a single failure that didn't reproduce in four further runs; I didn't capture which test it was.
- **Python client**: 174 passed. 3 tests are new, and `test_httpx_kwargs` was updated to patch the transport sse_v4 uses.
- **JS client**: browser mode 198 passed and 10 skipped; Node mode 183 passed and 25 skipped. 7 tests are new, in `submit_v4.test.ts`.
- **`js/core` unit tests**: 49 passed.
- **Playwright, full suite without reload specs**: 202 passed and 1 failed. The failure, `audio_debugger.spec.ts › recording audio`, also fails on unmodified `7.0-dev` in my environment, because of the fake microphone.
- **Linters**: `ruff` is clean. `ty` reports nothing in changed files; its remaining diagnostics are unresolved imports of packages I didn't install. `svelte-check` reports 16 errors, all in files this PR doesn't touch.

- [x] I used AI (Claude Code) to write the code, the tests and this description. This draft still needs a full human review.

prs.title: [No Merge] Gradio 7.0
prs.body:
## Description

Tracking PR for Gradio 7.0. **Do not merge** until the launch. Same setup as the Gradio 6.0 tracking PR (#11908).

`7.0-dev` is the integration branch for Gradio 7 work. Open Gradio 7 PRs against `7.0-dev`, not `main`. The `previews-build` workflow runs on this PR, so every push to `7.0-dev` produces a preview wheel for testing (see the preview comment below for the `pip install` link).

CI changes on this branch (revert the ones marked † before merging to `main`):
- Shared install actions (`install-all-deps`, `install-frontend-deps`) are referenced at `@7.0-dev` instead of `@main`
- Preview wheels are versioned `7.0.0.dev0`, not the latest PyPI version: `previews-build` uses `changes@7.0-dev`, and that action hardcodes the version
- The Python dependency cache key uses a `gradio-lib-7.0-dev-` prefix, so it doesn't collide with `main`'s cache
- Branch-push workflows (functional, js, hygiene, storybook, semgrep) run on `7.0-dev` instead of the stale `5.0-dev`
- PRs targeting `7.0-dev` get changesets generated, like PRs targeting `main`

Not set up yet: `publish.yml` does not run on `7.0-dev`, and changesets are not in pre-release mode, so nothing is published to PyPI or npm from this branch.

Milestone: [Gradio 7 Launch](https://github.com/gradio-app/gradio/milestone/41) (see the issues there)

prs.title: Run history: record to the caller's own bucket, from a custom frontend or via the host platform
prs.body: Two things that turn out to be the same feature: a `gr.Server` app whose custom frontend manages its own history, and a gradio app on Spaces that records a visitor's runs into **their** bucket — not the developer's — without anyone signing in. ## Why Run history could already be written to a Hub bucket, but only by an app holding a token that could *act as the user*. That works for a local app, a self-hosted one, or an explicit OAuth sign-in. It does not cover the two cases here: - **`gr.Server`** has no components and no settings UI, so there is nothing to pick a destination with and nothing to render a past run from. Today a `gr.Server` on a Space records nothing at all. - **A gradio app on Spaces** has no credential for its visitors and should not be handed a broad one. The Spaces proxy is explicit about this: `ip_token_middleware` strips what the browser sent before forwarding, because a Space runs code its visitors never agreed to trust. ## What **One option and one method on the client:** ```js const app = await Client.connect(origin, { history_bucket: "alice/badge-history" }); await app.read_history(); // { bucket?, limit? }, assets resolved to fetchable URLs app.options.history_bucket = id; // repoint later calls ``` No setup call and no write call. Writing needs no endpoint — `history_bucket` rides the `x-gradio-history-bucket` header submit already sent, and the server writes the record from the run it actually executed, so records stay server-attested. Connecting needs no endpoint either: `save_record` already calls `ensure_bucket`, so the first run recorded to a bucket creates it. On the platform path there is no bucket for the caller to name, so `read_history()` may be called with none. **Two ways a credential reaches the app, one sink behind them:** | | delegated | platform-minted | |---|---|---| | used when | the caller handed this app a token (local, self-hosted, OAuth) | the caller handed over nothing (a Space visitor) | | bucket | the caller's choice | the platform's, one per user per app | | scope | whatever the caller's token has | that one bucket, no repo creation | | gradio code | `save_record` / `list_records` | the same | `resolve_target` prefers the delegated credential — signing in and naming a bucket is a choice, and a platform default must not quietly override it. The two halves are never mixed: a minted token against a bucket the caller named would only ever be refused. Reads resolve identically, so a run is never recorded somewhere it cannot be read back from. **Three prerequisites**, each a bug in its own right: 1. **The mocked local-dev OAuth token broke history outright.** Off Spaces, `attach_oauth` mocks the login routes and puts `"mock-oauth-token-for-local-dev"` in the session; `resolve_token` returned it and short-circuited the loopback fallback, so it went to the Hub and 401'd. Signing in locally was *worse* than not signing in. 2. **`gr.Server` could not do OAuth at all.** `expects_oauth` keys off a `LoginButton`, and Server mode has no components, so `/login/huggingface` never mounted. Added `Server.launch(oauth=True)`. 3. **`GRADIO_APP_ID`** pins the app id, which is otherwise random per process. Runs are filed under it, so every restart orphans everything saved before it. Opt-in; **the most droppable part of this PR** if it reads as scope creep. ## Demo `demo/server_run_history/` — a `gr.Server` with a custom frontend: sign in with HF, name a bucket, run endpoints, click a past run to repopulate the page. One endpoint returns a file, so the asset round-trip is exercised. ## Verification **Delegated path**, locally against real buckets: signed in, ran both endpoints, **reloaded the page**, clicked a past run and got the text, palette and image back — the image served from the bucket proxy, not a local temp file. Restarted the server and the history survived. Pointed at a bucket that did not exist and confirmed one run created it. **Platform path**, end to end against the real Hub, with a middleware attaching the two headers the way the proxy would, on a plain `gr.Interface` configured with no bucket of its own: ``` in bucket: ['runs/platform-demo/note/017895983545213860006ebd4eea.json'] read back: 200 1 record(s) record: note [{'__asset__': 'a001.txt'}] asset: 200 b'note: ship it' ``` `test/test_history.py` 31 passing, client 181 node / 196 browser, SPA builds. ## Known wrinkles - **No "record written" signal.** `predict()` returning doesn't mean the record exists — the write is fire-and-forget — and bucket listings cache for 30s, so a run can need a second refresh to appear. The demo refreshes at 800ms and 3s. - **Dropping the setup call costs error feedback.** If a bucket id is wrong or the user lacks `manage-repos`, runs silently don't save. `read_history()` is a partial probe (401 means sign in) but cannot detect a write-scope problem, since a nonexistent bucket reads the same as an empty one. A frontend that cares can still import `connect_bucket()`; the built-in UI does. - Gradio serves SVG as `application/octet-stream; attachment` from both the file route and the asset proxy, so SVG outputs won't render in an ``. The demo uses PNG. --- ## What this needs from the Spaces side Nothing here ships the platform half. Gradio is written against the contract below; none of it exists yet. It is deliberately two headers and no service, so that the record format stays entirely inside gradio and changing it never needs a deploy on your side. ### 1. Attach two headers on requests into a Space ``` X-HF-History-Bucket: /history-- X-HF-History-Token: ``` Gradio uses them only as a pair, and only when the caller has not connected a bucket of their own. Absent either header, nothing changes anywhere. ### 2. One bucket per user per Space, and a token scoped to it This is the part that makes handing a Space a real credential defensible, and it is not optional. If every Space wrote into one shared `alice/gradio-history`, a read-capable token given to any Space would let it read **every prompt and output that user has ever sent to any Space**. Per-Space buckets mean a leaked token buys its holder the history of the app they were already using, and nothing else. The token needs write **and read** — reading is how a returning visitor gets their history back — and should not be able to create repos, which is the scope you described as `contribute-buckets`. Gradio skips `ensure_bucket` for a minted credential precisely so it never asks for a power the token was narrowed to exclude. ### 3. Pre-create the bucket Follows from the above: the Space cannot create it. Creating it at mint time is the natural place. ### 4. Make the token stable for a while, not per request Gradio caches bucket listings for 30s keyed partly on the token, and a token that changes on every request means the cache never hits — every history read becomes a full bucket listing plus a download per record. A token minted per session with a sane TTL (minutes, not seconds) avoids that. This also sidesteps the problem that killed the earlier design: a credential captured when the request arrives is still valid when a slow generative run finishes and the record is finally written. ### 5. Asset size policy `externalize_assets` caps a single remote asset at 64MB and a run can carry several, so the bucket needs a per-user quota and a failure gradio can log without failing the run. ### 6. A product decision, not an implementation detail This records every prompt and output a visitor sends to any Space into their Hub account, silently, with no click. Scoping makes it defensible; it does not make it not a policy decision. It needs an opt-out and somewhere a user can see and delete what has been kept. 🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)
